subtopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I was one of those who asked that this bill be sent to the appropriate committee for consideration. There is nothing in the bill which under the present way of doing things is particularly objectionable, but personally I oppose the idea of mortgage and insurance companies having full control of all the investment funds of Canada. However. perhaps this is not tihe moment to fight that.
There is only one part of the bill to which I take objection, and I want to register my protest now. It is covered by a certain section of the bill which I suppose I cannot refer to now' because we are not on that section.

subtopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: What section is it?

subtopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Section 7, subsection 2,
permits companies to split their shares. I have always been opposed to that, and I cannot see any need for it with companies of this kind. It may well be, as was pointed out by someone in the committee, that this provision will not be used, but the fact that these companies are permitted to do it is something to which I want to take objection. Everyone knows that once shares are split there is an immediate tendency for the price of the shares to increase. The excuse is put forward that this is done in order that poorer people may make investment. If they do make investment, under these circumstances 83166-354
they are buying at a higher price, and if they are ever to receive a profit on their investment, higher charges will have to be made to the public who borrow money. Moreover, this may be used as a cover-up for higher profits; I understand that that kind of practice is not uncommon. I just want to say that I am opposed to that section of the bill and to the principle which allows private corporations to manage the whole investment of Canadian funds.

subtopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: This matter came up the other evening in connection with the amalgamation of two existing trust companies which I opposed on account of the lack of any public control of these trust companies in their methods of handling these. The time has come when the definition should be changed because these trusts and combines and restraints of trade are flourishing like a green bay tree in Canada at present. The objection I have is that the changes in definition in the act do not go far enough. Trust companies in the different provinces are being united and large splits of capital are being made for the benefit of the existing shareholders who haire advance notice of what is going to be done. This has been happening very extensively in recent days. I know I have seen advertisements in the newspapers giving notice of this action by mergers of these trust companies soon to become a monopoly. They are handing out stock split up at par and sold to the public at 125. There should be further legislation to give more control of these national trust companies. 'The board of directors is being increased from twenty-one to thirty by this act, and when the number of directors is increased like that, the directors do not direct at all and control is under one central management. The trust company business has been a great success in this country and no doubt is a more efficient method of handling estates, but the time has come when there should be more regulation of this business in the public interest. There should be control of mergers and the issue of capital stock, which often permits the cutting of a huge melon running into millions, for the benefit of the few.

speechtext: The house resumed from Saturday, July 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. McCann for the second reading of Bill No. 453, to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CREDITING TO C.B.C. GROSS AMOUNT OF MONEYS RECEIVED FROM LICENCE FEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this debate was adjourned on Saturday 1 had just indicated some reasons why we were opposed to the granting of this $544,000 to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. One of the reasons I gave was that I feel that the C.B.C. in its present set-up is

too much subject to political interference, and I want to enlarge on that for a moment.
It is not only the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself but the whole sphere of radio broadcasting, the issuing of licences and the whole field of radio in Canada that I have in mind. In other words I do not merely confine my remarks or intend them to apply only to the chairman and board of governors as being subject to political influence, but I say that the complicated set-up we have of three departments all interested in radio and the various steps that must be taken between the application for a licence to broadcast and the granting of such licence, leaves room for political interference. As I said, I dlo not intend to let it rest there, because I do not think that would be proper. I will cite instances in support of my contention that this state of affairs exists and that it should be changed in any event, but certainly changed before we approve the granting of any further money to the corporation.	,
During the sittings of the radio committee it was alleged that in the choice of news commentators those favourable to government policy were favoured over those unfavourable to government policy, and that in the broadcasting of news by the C.B.C. there were occasions when political considerations were borne in mind. I want to cite an instance of that last statement.
On Tuesday, July 8, there was a very important debate in this house on the Civil Sendee Act. It was suggested that merchant seamen should !be given a preference under that act, and other veterans' benefits. A motion was made to that effect which led to a division of the house. In the debate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and three other ministers of the crown intervened!. It was the occasion of one of the closest divisions of the session. The motion to extend these benefits to merchant seamen was rejected as a result-

speechtext:
My opposition to this
measure is based largely on the fact that the present set-up is subject to political influence, and I am now seeking to support that statement. I go further than that and say that not only is it subject to political influence but when we seek the true reasons behind some of the decisions which are made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, or the licensing authority, these reasons are suppressed and the full information is not made available to members of the committee-
During the proceedings of the committee on Friday, June 27, I made reference to the granting of a licence to station CFRA in Ottawa. The situation behind that, Mr. Speaker, is this. An application was made before June of 1945 for a licence for an additional radio station in Ottawa. That application was turned down. After June of 1945, which was, you will recall, the date of the last general election, three applications were submitted, amongst them one by the same man who had made .the previous application. After June of 1945 the application for a licence was granted to the person who had been turned down previously. I referred to this matter in the committee and asked for a copy of the
Canadian Broadcasting Act

briefs submitted in support of the application, because I had been given to understand that one' of the unsuccessful applicants had submitted the best brief that had ever been submitted in support of an application for a radio licence. Therefore I wanted to get the briefs, and I also asked the chairman of the board of governors if he could tell me why this individual who was previously turned down should, a few months later, be given approval of his licence to broadcast. I received no satisfactory explanation. I suggested in the committee that it was because this individual was the radio publicity manager for the Liberal campaign, particularly the Prime Minister's campaign, in the last election and had been the cheer leader at the Prime Minister's last meeting here in Ottawa on June 8. The fact was questioned, Mr. Speaker, by the chairman of the committee. He asked whether that was true or not. Since he questioned it I read to the committee a report of the meeting from the Ottawa Journal, which reads as follows:
Five minutes before Mr. King spoke, a Montreal man, Frank Ryan, explained to the crowd how to applaud "to make it sound good." They must, he instructed, start the applause with a short sharp burst, sustain the volume and then cut it off abruptly. "You must clap loudly," he advised, "to show that you have plenty of enthusiasm." At that one of the hecklers in the upper seats shouted: "But we haven't any enthusiasm, Bud." During the .early stages of Mr. King's address, and at its conclusion. Mr. Ryan "cued" the applause. To bring it up he swept his hands up from the floor and pushed them above his head. And to cut the applause, he flattened his hands in the manner of a college cheer-leader "ending a ..stunt."
I asked the chairman of the board of governors whether these facts had any influence on the granting to Mr. Ryan of his licence. He said no, so far as the C.B.C. itself was concerned. I asked him for an explanation of why this man who had previously been refused his licence should subsequently be granted it, and in my submission, as is supported by the report of the proceedings, he was not able to give that explanation. I asked him for a copy of the briefs tabled in support of the various applications so that we might have an opportunity to compare them to see whether Mr. Ryan's application was a better one than the others. That will be found on page 497 of the committee's proceedings. I asked Mr. Dunton this question:
By Mr. Fulton:
Q. May I repeat my request for the other two briefs?-A. I have a copy of Mr. Freiman's brief which, again. I would ask to have back because it is the file copy. I have a copy of the endorsations for Mr. Shearer. I do not think Mr. Shearer had any written brief.
JMr. Fulton.]
Before I go any further I charge that the documents we asked for were, firstly, suppressed and secondly, when they were tabled they were distorted. I ask the house to listen carefully to the reply made by Mr. Dunton:
I have a copy of the endorsations for Mr. Shearer. I do not think Mr. Shearer had any written brief. He presented his arguments orally and supported them, with copies of endorsations from various organizations who thought there should be another station.
Q. You say he did not submit an engineering brief?-A. When I refer to a "brief" now, I am using it in the sense of arguments and reasons why a person should have a licence, not a technical brief. These briefs dealt with considerations as to why there should be a station and why these people should be the people to have it.

speechtext:
I merely want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I feel that the privileges which have been granted to the private stations over the years have accumulated to the extent of endangering the whole future of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I regretted that there were some recommendations in the report of the committee which made a further step in the direction of interference with the nationally-owned system. I have reference particularly to the extension of the licence for a period of three years. I think that is a mistake; I believe it places the private stations in a position which was not contemplated either when the Aird report was made or when the various parliamentary committees reported to this house from time to time. I feel that we are now suffering from an accumulation of weaknesses on the part of the broadcasting corporation to whom we entrusted the authority with regard to broadcasting in this country! Step by step, year by year, one can trace the granting of further bits of privilege; the kilowatt power of a private station increased, and so on, until today, contrary to the very fundamentals of the radio and broadcasting acts, the private stations believe they have an unlimited vested right in public property, that is, in wave lengths. That point of view has been placed before the public through advertising and various forms of propaganda during the sittings of the committee.
In my view the brief presented by the private broadcasting corporations was not a brief directed only against the method of operating the corporation under the departments; rather it was a criticism, a condemnation of our whole system of parliamentary and representative government, and I felt that the brief was written by people who had no appreciation of our British institutions and of the representative system under which we operate in this country. If we allowed the kind of organization to be set up which they propose in their brief we would be setting up in this country one of those organizations

which would lead us into what is popularly called throughout the world a fascist state.
So I regret that some of the recommendations by the committee were in the nature of giving further privileges. I am sorry, too, that the report seems at least to condone both multiple ownership, which I believe is a menace to freedom in this country, and the newspaper ownership of radio stations, which restricts the free control of news services. May I just add that I know from conversation'-and I repeat that-I know from conversation with at least two gentlemen who are members of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, the private interests, that while they are members of that organization they did not agree with the brief or the recommendations contained in the brief. I have since learned) that there are other stations in much the same position; but in spite of their belief that the C.A.B. is more or less dominated by one or two powerful radio stations in this country, and because they need certain services which the C.A.B. gives them, they diid not like to come before the committee or to dissociate themselves from the representations wdrich were made mainly I believe on behalf of several large stations or groups in this country.
A moment ago I said I was not going to make a long speech. I have referred briefly to matters which I think are of fundamental importance in the radio field. I regret that something was not done to order the divorce of radio stations from newspaper ownership, and to break up those monopolies which are growing up in relation to multiple ownership. In this province we have one group owning or operating some six or eight radio stations, I believe; and the kind of service they give at Kirkland Lake, Timmins and other places, with the advertising all day long, the use of recordings, and the way those stations are operated, have caused the people in those districts to complain. And may I add that in this province of Ontario there is another very legitimate complaint. That is that we have one important part of this province where there is not proper coverage by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I refer to the Windsor area, where there is one powerful station, CKLW, wdiich is advertised throughout the United States as "CKLW, Windsor and Detroit" and is classified in United States lists of broadcasting stations as an American station. As I said to the committee when I was there on one occasion the people of that city resent very greatly the fact that over that station they cannot get the news summaries of the Canadian Broadcasting Corpora-

Canadian Broadcasting Act
tion, but they do get news commentaries from the American side. One of the reasons this broadcasting corporation was set up years ago, when the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was in power in this country, to some extent was to safeguard our radio from domination by our great, powerful and friendly neighbour to the south. I say to the minister and through him to the board of governors of the broadcasting corporation that they should make every effort to establish in the Windsor area a station that will give the service the people of that area require, and which will be a thoroughly Canadian station with sufficient coverage for the area that should be covered from that point.

I think I got an explanation of that. "Yes," they said, " we like the private station at certain times and would not like to do without it, because we get something over the private stations that we do not get over C.B.C. The C.B.C. programmes are fine and we like them. Mr. Speaker, I am not. a member of the radio committee. I remember when I was a member of the House of Commons in 1936 the Conservative government under Mr. Bennett introduced a bill regarding this corporation. I object to the principle of the bill before us for three or four reasons and my objections are these. You are handing over this money to the government-controlled radio. The auditor general has no control over it because the corporation have their own auditors. As for the board of directors, they are a political board and always have been. The only one who was not, Fred Crawford, was one of our leading citizens in Toronto who was greatly interested in community and social work of all kinds, a sportsman and a good business man all combined, one of our most popular citizens.
What are you going to do by this act? If you pass this bill the House of Commons washes its hands of any control over this corporation. In the first place this corporation has not sufficient business capacity to handle the job. I got a return brought down in the house the year before last and last year as to the number of prosecutions, by provinces, for failure to pay the licence fee of $2.50. The fee should be abolished altogether. If you are going to have a monopoly corporation you should have a free system. That should have been done long ago. I can tell you this, that the return I got in 1945 and 1946 showed that 70 per cent of the prosecutions were taking place in our city; in Ottawa and Hull there were practically no prosecutions and few in

any of the other provinces. When the money provided by this bill is turned over to the corporation we have no longer any control over it. If you want a radio board why do you not have an independent board like the transport commission? You might just as well hand control of the C.P.R. over to the C.N.R. as to appoint a board like this.
Our city has been a dumping ground for employees of the broadcasting corporation since it was set up. I do not blame the present minister because he has a very likeable personality in my opinion-although I am only one. I do not blame him for what is going on. I blame nobody except the high court of parliament for taking control every session out of the hands of parliament. I remember what went on in radio before the war. Everybody who was a pacifist was hired as a commentator over the radio. It was ridiculous. All these commentators were political appointments.
I do not blame the C.C.F. for wanting this and for wanting these commentators, but I say to them that if we pass this bill we shall make the broadcasting corporation a public monopoly, and the auditor general will be nowhere. He will have no control over the expenditure of that money, nor will parliament; they will say it is statutory now and refuse to give us any information. They must be pretty hard up, this corporation, and they are going to get still further hard up. When I see the waste that is going on in their purchasing of property in Toronto, at this time when there is such a shortage of houses, I am shocked. They are bringing people into Toronto from all over Canada from Vancouver to Halifax. These people do not belong to our city. They are being given good big jobs and some of them have very little to do. I remember a man called John Fisher, being brought into Toronto from Halifax. He had been attacking our city for years because of its political leanings. He was brought to Toronto. He has nothing much to do. He can occupy his time with his private interests on the radio for advertisers, boosting advertising, and so on. He is not the only one. They are bringing them in by the dozen, but I do not know of a Toronto citizen who can get a position with C.B.C. I do not know any of the directors or top officials of C.B.C. except that one very good man to whom I referred a moment ago. I paid my .$2.50 and shut the radio off and did not turn it on for six months. It is 
simply ridiculous. I remember on a Good Friday they were putting on jazz and all that kind of thing, on one of the greatest days in the Christian church. But they forgot all about that. I do not criticize them so much because there is no doubt they have some good programmes, but they are Washington-minded.
With all the advertising we have they are going to have a dictatorship; there will be no public control. We have one or two private stations in our city. No one has spoken to me about this bill. I have not had one person speak to me. I went down to the radio committee one morning to see one of our members. There was a big sign on the door marked "private". A messenger came to the door and told me it was private, that I had no business to go in, so I did not go in. I did not even attempt to enter the room. That is what happened. I never saw such nepotism in my life as exists in Toronto radio. They bring in their sisters, their cousins, their aunts and their uncles; they come from Halifax and Vancouver. That is the kind of commission we have.
The same thing applies to sports on the radio. Some of the individuals were never sportsmen at all. If we adopt this measure you can say goodbye to any public control of radio by the high court of parliament. It is no wonder that people are criticizing the House of Commons. In the dying days of the session a matter like this is brought up. The same thing is true of foreign affairs and everything else. They are all brought up in the dying hours of the session and1 are given five minutes' attention. We might just as well not be here at all. The committee was appointed early in the session and did not meet until after Easter, and then this came on. I do not mind my friends to the left getting up and speaking in favour of it. I am not objecting to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) speaking in favour of this bill. I spoke to the Minister of National Defence one night, when the hon. member was going over to Moscow, to pacify Russia, and11 told him he ought to send a bodyguard to ensure that he would get back; I was afraid he might be kidnapped. I am glad to see him here today.
I am not going to say any more. If the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Henderson) will second my motion I shall move the six months hoist to this bill. Since I should1 like to see the house close on Wednesday morning I shall not say any more at this time. I do not see how the Liberal party and a government which believes in responsible government can bring in a measure like

this giving this corporation absolute control of radio broadcasting. The commission has done nothing about aids to education in our public, separate and secondary schools. In England the British Broadcasting Corporation have done a great deal along that line.
As I said a while ago, not one single person has spoken to me about this bill.

I am not going to apologize for rising to speak on this bill at this time because I regard it as a matter of importance. It is not the fault of anyone on this side that for the second year in succession this matter has been left to what we all hope are the dying moments of the session. I think it is a great pity; it is a matter of great importance, and at any rate I am going to have my brief say today.
I am against the bill, not because I do not want to see the C.B.C. get a good show. I do want to see it get a good show. I have no desire whatever to see it cramped or hampered or badly treated, but I think this is the wrong way to give the money.
In his statement the minister confined himself, and properly so, to a mere statement of the reasons for the need of money and the adequacy of this means of raising the money. The minister did not go farther afield and deal, as some other hon. members have, with some of the more important questions which I submit underlie this. I want to refer briefly to these and in particular to one of them. I am not going to deal with a wide variety of subjects.
To my mind it is of great importance indeed to have what the committee report calls a "separate regulating board." Up to the present in this debate I think it is fair to say there has been no justification even attempted of that stand. The two persons who have referred to it are the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart)-and if I do not do him an injustice what he said was that he thought it would be worse to have the Canadian Association of Broadcasters in control than to have the C.B.C. I would not argue with him on that point because so far as I know nobody suggests that the Canadian Association of Broadcasters should be put in control. All that is being suggested is that we should have an independent body, and that is what I want to speak about. The other person who referred to this was the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). While he did not commit
himself to an independent board-because he said his mind was open on the subject, he said there had been difficulties with regard to the transport board-nevertheless he did indicate great dissatisfaction with the report of the committee.
Incidentally may I draw particularly to the attention of the house the arresting statement which was made with regard to the hon. member for New Westminster. Somebody to my left referred to him as the one just man, in the Liberal party. I think he said the one just man in the Liberal party or the one honest man. I wish to point out that I looked up the book of Genesis yesterday and I found that Abraham in his trafficking with the Almighty got to the point where Sodom and Gomorrah would have been saved had there been ten just men in those cities. It did not get any lower than that. I submit that the Liberal party is in very great difficulty if it has only one just man in the party.

I want to make a brief reference to a separate regulating board. This is what the report said:
In the result, your committee is not prepared at the present time to suggest any fundamental: change in radio regulation. The national broadcasting system is still in the transitional and developmental stage and the principles underlying its institution have the same force to-day as when the decision to establish it was made. Notwithstanding arguments advanced we do not feel justified under all the circumstances ino recommending a fundamental change now.
I submit therefore that this, to me, very important matter, more important than anything else in this discussion, has not even been argued. There has been no reason given, so far as I am aware, against this board. My feeling is that the reasons in favour of it are more strong now, and that they are just as much in the interest of the C.B.C. as they are in the interests of the private stations, and that is why I am in favour of this independent board.
The report itself is a disappointing document; it seems an apologetic document. It says that there is not much competition and that the operators are making money. To me the whole tenor of the report is apologetic. We have further the definite statement from the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) indicating the very unsatisfactory manner in
55(56
Canadian Broadcasting Act

which the report was arrived at, and that to my mind greatly accentuates what to me was the unsatisfactory present situation, and which I think is quite properly described by saying that the CJB.C. at the present time is judge and policeman, and somebody said executioner as well.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) referred to the Canadian National Railways. I want to carry it one step further. He said it would be very unfair if the Canadian National Railways should be not only an operator but should control and dictate the whole railway policy of Canada. I go further than that and suggest that nobody would suggest that the Canadian National Railways should be put in that position. I should be very much surprised if anybody would suggest that. Why is it we have this situation in broadcasting? Why is it that what ordinarily would be regarded as the fair thing is not being done?
I made some inquiries and as far as I can discover the only reason is that in the early thirties when this was instituted-and incidentally the name of the former leader of this party was extensively quoted a year ago as having favoured it, which I believe he did -I am informed that at that time the guiding reason was that it was feared unless we appeared as a government, unless it was a government monopoly, we might not get anything like a fair share of the wave lengths. That was the reason which directed it at that time. Whatever may or may not be the reason then, so far as I can understand the situation, that reason has disappeared. We now have some kind of judicial allotment of wave lengths as between the countries, and therefore I suggest that we can go back to what I believe is the fair way and the only way of dealing with this situation. As things are at present we run into the situation where you have many of the evils of a monopoly.
I submit that uncontrolled monopoly is a bad thing. It is a bad thing if it is private monopoly, and in a way it is worse if it is government monopoly, because then unfortunately no one believes, at least a great many people do not believe, that it is entirely uncontrolled by government. Therefore I submit that makes an additional reason for setting up an independent board.
To me it is a great disappointment that this "matter has not even been discussed. It is important. There has been no speech on the *opposite side apart from the minister's, except bv the hon. member for New Westminster, who was critical. We have had no expression of views from the other side, and I do not 
believe for a moment that there are not people sitting opposite who have a feeling in favour of an independent board. It seems to me therefore that the situation we have here is nothing but a running away from the discussion of this question. No serious attempt has been made to raise" any question. The member for Rosetown-Biggar made an interesting speech in which he referred to various abuses which he thought might creep in, and all the time he was speaking I was thinking the best way of removing that feeling was to have an independent board, so that there might be no suspicion at all that the government interferes with its creature.
I want to say a word as to the bill itself. I began by saying that I was the last person who would wish to see the C.B.C. starve. I want to see it generously dealt with. But I submit that for reasons already given this is the wrong way to go about it. This is an indirect way which can only lead to misunderstandings and difficulties of various kinds. If the government wishes to give them further money, as it very well might, it should make a grant in the ordinary way and not adopt this indirect way, which defies all laws of good business and good governmental procedure as well.

speechtext:
Hon. COLIN GIBSON (Secretary of State, for the Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 18, to adjust the representation in the House of Commons.
Motion agreedi to and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.
Mr. GIBSON (Hamilton West); Mr. Chairman, in considering the report of the special committee on redistribution I should like first of all to pay a tribute to the chairman and also the members of that committee. While not a member of the committee myself I understand' the members worked together in a spirit of good will and a desire for fair play. The chief electoral officer has informed me that never in his experience has he seen such harmony as existed at the meetings of this committee; and I think this statement will be supported by such experienced members as the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol).
As the report of the committee shows, the members were unanimous in their recommendations as to the amendments to sections 4 and 7 of the bill and. as to the schedules relating to New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan and. Alberta. The report, though not unanimous as to section 2 and the schedules of the other provinces, according to the report of the special committee represents a very substantial measure of agreement. For the benefit of the members of the house who were not members of the special committee I should like to outline the main changes that have been recommended in the various provinces.
fMr. Knowles.]
British Columbia receives two- additional seats under redistribution. The members of the British Columbia subcommittee unanimously agreed that these seats be created in the lower mainland area, one within Vancouver city to be called Vancouver-Quadra, and the other a suburban seat composed of the municipalities of Burnaby, Richmond and Coquitlam, now part of New Westminster and Vancouver North, and called Bumaby-Rich-mond. As the remaining part of Vancouver North contains no part of the city of Vancouver, it has been renamed Coast-Capilano, describing the two principal districts of the riding. The only other change in the British Columbia seats is the transfer of that part of the present Cariboo riding which is south of the 52 degrees 30 minutes parallel, to the Kamloops riding. The present Cariboo riding is the largest in the province, and lies on both sides of the Rocky Mountains. A measure of relief has been provided by the transfer of the southern part of the riding to the adjacent and much smaller Kamloops riding.
Saskatchewan loses one seat, and a seat was eliminated in the southern part of the province, which was the drought area. Since 1931 a large number of people have left this section and settled, to a considerable extent, in the more northerly part of the province. It was not only necessary to consider the elimination of one seat in the southern part, but also the question of moving the limits of most constituencies further to the north. The Saskatchewan sub-committee brought in a unanimous report.
There were no changes made in Alberta.
Manitoba loses one seat, but changes in population made it desirable to have a rather extensive alteration in the limits of the constituencies. The present ridings of Lisgar and Macdonald were combined and the present ridings of Portage la Prairie and Neepawa were also combined. This permitted the establishment of a new constituency out of part of Selkirk and the suburban area of Winnipeg to be known as Selkirk. The remainder of the former constituency of Selkirk will be known as Norquay.
The representation of Ontario is increased by one, and this seat was allotted to northern Ontario. In addition the committee decided to allot an additional seat to northern Ontario, and this was found by combining the district of Muskoka with the present constituency of Parry Sound, and by annexing the remainder of Muskoka-Ontario to the present constituencies of Victoria and Ontario. In order to reduce the population of Ottawa West, which was over 94,000, the southerly part of the

Redistribution
riding was transferred to the riding of Carle-ton. In order to reduce the population of Ottawa East the town of Eastview was transferred to the riding of Russell. One township now in Peterborough West was transferred to Northumberland, with a result that the whole of Northumberland county is now together for electoral purposes. The township of Markham and the villages of Stouffville and Markham were transferred from York East to York North. The town of Weston was transferred from York South to York West. The township of Burford was transferred from Brant to Brantford. The remainder of the riding of Brant was combined with the townships of Beverly, Ancaster, Glanford and Bin-brook from Wentworth to form a new constituency of Brant-Wentworth. The township of Logan including the town of Mitchell was transferred from Perth to Huron-Perth. The township of Biddulph and the town of Lucan were transferred from Middlesex East to Middlesex West. The townships of Tilbury West and Sandwich South were transferred from Essex North to Essex South. The township of, Oro was transferred from Simcoe North to Simcoe East. The township of Baxter was transferred from Muskoka-Ontario to Simcoe East. In northern Ontario, the present ridings of Nipissing, Timiskaming and Cochrane have been rearranged into five seats known as Nipissing, Timiskaming, Cochrane, Timmins and Sudbury.
Quebec gained eight seats on redistribution, and in addition to allotting these, it was necessary for the committee to readjust many of the existing boundaries in view of the changes in population. The committee recom-mendedi the elimination of the existing constituency of Laval-Two Mountains so there were nine new seats to be allotted. The committee has recommended that four of these be allotted to the island of Montreal, the new constituencies being known as Laval, Lafon-taine, Mount Royal and Papineau. The committee also recommends the creation of a new riding of Villeneuve out of the northern portion of Pontiac; a new constituency known as Lapointe out of the western half of Chicoutimi; the present constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay was divided into separate constituencies of Charlevoix and Saguenay; and the present constituency of Lac St. Jean-Roberval was divided into separate constituencies . of Lac St. Jean and Roberval. In addition, the Magdalen Islands are allotted a separate seat in view of the fact that these islands are 150 miles from Gaspe, to which they had been attached for electoral purposes.
In New Brunswick and. Prince Edward Island no changes were made.
Nova Scotia is entitled to one additional seat on redistribution. This was provided by joining the municipalities of Queens and Shelburne to form a constituency to be named Queens-Shelburne. No changes were made in the island of Cape Breton other than the joining of Hillside and South Forks, which previously formed part of the constituency of Cape Breton South, to the constituency of Cape Breton North-Victoria. It was recommended by the committee that the dual constituency of Halifax be divided into two separate constituencies. Since the bringing in of the report of the special committee strong representations have been received from Halifax that the city and county of Halifax be continued as a dual constituency. In view of these representations I intend to move at the proper time that items 8 and 9 of the Nova Scotia schedule be deleted so as to leave the Halifax constituencies unaltered.
The special committee has also recommended that under the provisions of section 51, subsection 2 of the British North America Act 1867-1946, that part of the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories lying west of 109th meridian of west longitude be added to the Yukon territory for electoral purposes to form a constituency known as Yukon-Mackenzie River.
While some of the members will find their constituencies altered, or in a few cases either combined or eliminated, I feel sure that they will realize that these changes have become necessary due to changed conditions, and in order to carry out the spirit and the provisions of the British North America Act. In conclusion I would move;
'That items 8 and 9 of the Nova Scotia schedule be deleted and that the following be substituted therefor:
"8. Halifax consisting of the city of Halifax and the county of Halifax, which shall return two members."
And that the subsequent items of the schedule be renumbered accordingly.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to say a word about the proposed redistribution in so far as it affects my own province of British Columbia, and then go on to make a few remarks with regard to the other features of the proposed redistribution of electoral seats. The Secretary of State has intimated to the committee that British Columbia is getting two additional seats, bringing our total to 18. One of those new seats is to be in the city of Vancouver and the other in the suburban area surrounding that city.
At the present lime Vancouver has four seats, Vancouver Centre, Vancouver-Burrardi, Vancouver East and Vancouver South. The
Redistribution

changes that are being made are to cut off a small portion of Vancouver Centre and Vancouver-Burrard and add them to the present Vancouver East; then to take the southern portion of Vancouver East and add it to Vancouver South, which is the largest seat in population, and divide that into two seats, a new Vancouver South and a seat to be known as Vaneouver-Quadra. The feature about this division is that the boundary line between the new Vancouver South and Vaneouver-Quadra is not a straight line.
A line should have been drawn across that portion of the city but the government supporters, led in so far as British Columbia is concerned by the hon. member for Vancouver North, saw fit to put a jog in that boundary with the result that the population of Vaneouver-Quadra will be considerably larger than that of the new Vancouver South. In my opinion there was no excuse for having a jog at all. The line should have been run straight across that portion of the city; in fact it could very well have been run along Thirty-third avenue which is the natural boundary between the ridings.

The jog between the new Vancouver South and Vaneouver-Quadra is in fact made for political purposes, in the vain hope of building up support for the government in the new Vancouver South. I do not think there is any dioubt as to the defeat the government candidate will get in that riding at the next election.
I should like to say a few words about the name of the new seat, Vaneouver-Quadra. I foresee that there may be much questioning after the next election when some one comes here as the hon. member for Vaneouver-Quadra. That is a name which means much on the whole Pacific coast. Quadra was a daring Spanish explorer on that coast. In 1775 two Spanish ships explored the coast as far north as Alaska and one of them was under the command of Quadra, who was then a naval lieutenant. Hon. members will be

interested to know the size of his ship. It was thirty-six feet in length, and had a twelve foot beam, which is not nearly as wide as the space from my desk to the desk opposite, with an eight foot depth of hold. As I have said, he went in that ship as far as Alaska. All but two members of his crew were stricken with scurvy, and finally Quadra himself had to climb the masts to look after the rigging. He was a bold explorer.
About twenty years later, in 1792, Quadra again visited the coast of British Columbia, this time as commander of what the Spanish called the settlement of Nootka on the west coast of the present Vancouver island. He was also in command of California and practically the whole western coast of North America. At Nootka, in 1792 he met Captain George Vancouver, who had been sent out from Great Britain to negotiate with the Spanish concerning a dispute as to who should own Nootka, the British or the Spanish. Another British explorer, Captain Cook, had been there in the intervening years between 1775 and 1792, and had obtained from the Indians sea-otter skins which were of great value on the Chinese market. As a result, different explorers had sailed for the west coast and trouble had arisen as to whether Nootka belonged to Spain or to Great Britain. By the way, Burrard is named after one of Captain Vancouver's officers.

Yes. Quadra and Vancouver met at Nootka and negotiated for a settlement of this dispute. They were unable to agree upon anything having to do with the dispute, but they became the warmest of friends. A few months later Quadra entertained Captain Vancouver off the coast of California, and the description given of him by Captain Vancouver is as follows:
He was the mainspring of a society that had produced so much happiness, who had rendered us so many essential benefits, and whose benevolence and disinterested conduct had impressed our minds with the highest esteem and veneration.
Actually Quadra named the present Vancouver island the island of Quadra and Vancouver, but eventually his name was dropped. So this name "Quadra" has a historical significance for those of us who are fortunate enough to live on the west coast of Canada, and we are very proud to have a riding named after this great explorer.
The other new riding is to be known as Bumaby-Richmond. It is in a suburban district around Vancouver. I have some-doubts whether the two main municipalities in that new riding have sufficient interests

Redistribution
in common to warrant putting them into one riding. However, we shall just have to see how it works out. It may be a very satisfactory riding.
My main point today concerning the British Columbia redistribution has to do with the Kamloops seat. That seat was created in 1933. It was a seat fitted into the main railway lines that run across the province. Along the Canadian Pacific railway it reaches from Ashcroft right through to Glacier, within fifty miles of the Alberta boundary. It also includes the main line of the Canadian National running up the Fraser valley and the valley of the Thompson to Kamloops and almost to the junction with the line that runs out. to Prince Rupert. It has been a big seat to cover. Kamloops city is pretty much the centre of the riding. One has to go back to Kamloops, if he is coming in from the east on the main line of the Canadian Pacific, to get up the main line of the C.N.R. It has been a difficult riding to cover. There is also quite a large area lying to the south of the main lines of these two railways.
The interests of the present riding are with the people who live to the south, in the present riding of Yale, not with the people who live to the north or to the west but primarily with the people who live to the south. The population of Kamloops riding in 1941 was 27.387. The population of Yale, lying south of that riding, was 51,874, almost twice as much. In fact, Yale is the biggest riding in the province outside of the ridings which include the larger cities. The fair way to add to the population of Kamloops would have been to take in the northern part of Yale.

The riding will now stretch from within fifty miles of the Alberta boundary to the heads of two of our great inlets on the sea coast, Jarvis inlet and Bute inlet. This change means that now Kamloops riding will have a population seven or eight thousand greater than the new Cariboo riding. That is on the 1941 census basis. On the ration book basis the difference will be much greater. The ration book figures are Kamloops, 35.098, Cariboo 38,657. The redistribution switches 10,031 from Cariboo to Kamloops and the result will be that Kamloops will have a ration-book population of 46,129 and Cariboo 28,626.
The result of this change is very" noticeable politically. Kamloops riding as I said was formed in 1933. In 1935 it was carried by T. J. O'Neill, the Liberal candidate, with a majority of 1,216 and in 1940 with a majority of 1,331. In 1945 the present member for Kamloops, Mr. Fulton, carried the riding by a majority of 177. The figures were, Fulton, 4,401, O'Neill, 4.224. McKenzie, C.C.F. 4,003, Codd, Labour Progressive 666.

The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), thirty-one years of age, led a company of our famous Seaforth Highlanders in action in Italy. He was mentioned in dispatches. He had a splendid record. Before that he was a Rhodes scholar. He was one of the outstanding young students of British Columbia. He is a young man who has made his mark right in this House of Commons in a way" that has not been equalled by any" other young man since I came here in 1936. His father sat in this house from 1917 to 1921. Before that he was a member

May I point out how the change has been made, and in so doing I would say that this constituency, as redefined, is a fine exemplification of what is meant by the w-ord "gerrymander." The word gerrymander in political parlance simply means that in redistributing a constituency the boundary lines are so altered as to do an obvious injury to one political party and give an obvious unfair political advantage to another party.
From that definition one would say that the Liberal party were obvious experts at gerrymandering. The member for Vancouver South told us what happened to certain members of the Progressive Conservative party. I do not like either the ideas or the principles of the Progressive Conservative party, even though I may have some regard for some of them as individuals in their private capacity, but I have a regard for justice, and I do not think that justice is ensured in this case. As the member for Vancouver South told us, four of the most prominent Tories are in grave danger of. losing their seats. In other words, the government intends to keep out of the house seventy-dive per cent of the fighting strength of the Tory' party, and one can only conclude that this is not chivalrous. The Prime Minister in the last debate had something to say about chivalry, in which I assume he is an expert. At page 5277 of Hansard of 1933 he made this statement:

but let me tell my hon. friends opposite it is not in accord with the sense of chivalry of the people of Canada as a whole. It may be Tory chivalry but it is neither British chivalry nor British fair play.
Let us make a comparison. The Tories were going to legislate out of existence one seat. The Liberals propose to get rid of four of the most prominent members of the Progressive Conservative party. One would assume then that there was a higher sense of chivalry in the Tories than in the Liberals, though I think that neither of them have the faintest idea of what is meant by British chivalry or British fair play. However, as the Prime Minister said in that debate fourteen years ago, the most important consideration is the political consideration, and this is being lived up to fully in this case. Justice and equity apparently have little to do with it.
Now I wish to refer to something nearer home so far as I am concerned, and that is the attempted gerrymander in the constituency of the member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplit-ny). I am not surprised, because the hon. member has been consistently a thorn in the side of the government. He has exposed the pretentions of their legislation on more than one occasion, and he has harried and harassed the members opposite. The situation is this. Here is a constituency which is already larger than most of the other rural ridings in Manitoba. The new piece which is added by this bill has a large Liberal majority, but the citizens who live there have really no relationship to the constituency of Dauphin. Their relationship is more to the towns of Neepawa and to Portage la Prairie. This is an obvious attempt on the part of the government to secure for themselves another seat, but let me assure them that they cannot do. They may as well give up Dauphm as a lost cause because the present member will be here in the next parliament.
There is another matter that perhaps affects me more personally. There has been a slight attempt at gerrymander in Winnipeg North. There is one section known as Elmwood, which is a geographic, social and cultural entity. In their wisdom and, I suspect, on instructions from Manitoba, the government decided to split this area in half and give one portion to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He needs it as a duck needs a third leg. In the last election all his opponents lost their deposits and, of course, that will happen again in the next election because he is inheriting a sound and wise C.C.F. majority. My objection is not to this area going to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but if anywhere I think it should have gone to the hon. member
for St. Boniface, for this area is contiguous to the constituency of St. Boniface. But if it had gone there we should have had another C.C.F. member for St. Boniface in the next house. It is quite obvious that the government has no desire whatsoever to see that happen, and they have stripped from me a certain majority and given it to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. As I say, it is a flagrant attempt at gerrymander; there can be no other word for it.
I wish to bring to the attention of the house some of the other things which the Prime Minister had to say fourteen years ago when he was in opposition. This I assume may have been Philip when sober.

A few months ago we introduced in this house an amendment suggesting that there should be an independent commission to define the constituency boundaries, and the house Liberal majority, with some Conservatives decided to vote it down. But first, I should like to read what the present Prime Minister had to say fourteen years ago about proportional representation, at page 5422 of Hansard:
I believe that the only true method of securing a representative parliament is by a system of proportional representation properly worked out with regard to the dominion as a whole. The reform should commence with the cities and the larger municipalities in our country. When the Liberal government was in office we introduced into this house a measure of proportional representation in connection with city constituencies. It was fought for some little time, there was considerable opposition from the then opposition and the measure was not proceeded with. It was not reintroduced because the government of the day had not a majority in the other chamber which would ensure its enactment, and there were more pressing matters requiring attention. I might add the late Liberal government did not have a majority in the senate all the time it was in office. If we had had a majority in the other house upon which we could have relied, we would have proceeded with our proportional representation measure.
For the last few years the Prime Minister has been appointing his own emissaries to the senate and having them sign on the dotted line. He had a majority which he could have used to that end, to secure P.R.. if he had reintroduced such legislation. It was not done. The then leader of the opposition goes on:
If we are ever returned to power a proportional representation measure will he a feature of the Liberal platform and programme of legislation.
That is another Liberal promise. The Liberals have been returned to power three times since and nothing at all has been said
Redistribution

or done on this issue. Then on page 5476, when the member for Bow River, Mr. Garland, was discussing this matter, he pointed out how certain Liberals had voted against proportional representation, and he said this:
I should like to ask the right hon. gentleman-
That is the present Prime Minister.
-if he has consulted those ministers and received their consent as well as the consent of these various genial French Canadian members to the legislation which he now proposes?
Mr. Mackenzie King: I might say that the matter has been discussed and agreed to in a Liberal caucus.
Later on Mr. Stevens, with prophetic wisdom, said, "They are just kidding the troops."
That, of course, has been amply proven.
Then I should like to read for the sake of the record what the Prime Minister said at page 5425-and it is interesting to see how his protestations stick up against his actions:
My own view, and I have come to it after observing pretty carefully what has been taking place and what has been said in debate in this house as well as in the corridors, is that redistribution should be taken out of the hands of the House of Commons, where the parties are immediately interested, and should be put into the hands of a commission of judges.
We advocated its being put into the hands of an independent commission, but the government turned it down. Then this is significant:
I would have that commission composed of judges selected in equal numbers by both sides of the house. The redistribution, if it is carried out in a fair way has not to do with party advantage at all.
That again was when the Prime Minister was leader of the opposition. He continues:
It ought to have solely to do with seeking to effect a fair and impartial division of the constituencies, and if three judges were named from one side of the house and three from the other, and if the choice were made, if you will, from among those who have been in polities and who therefore may be presumed to know something about conditions generally as they exist throughout the country, I think a redistribution which would be regarded as fair might be arrived at.
On various occasions the hon. member for Stanstead has objected to judges being in politics or being at times attacked in this house. I have sympathy with him. But I consider it a regrettable thing that the then leader of the opposition, now leader of the parliament of Canada, believes that judges who are in office should step off the bench, don again the political mantle, decide redistribution and go up to the bench once again, I suppose to be impartial. In the past the trouble with our judiciary has been that too

many politicians who have not made the grade in this house have become judges. So long as that happens, the judiciary will not be regarded with the respect which is due to it. Then at page 5468, I feel I must quote this:
Of one thing we can be perfectly sure: a very limited number of those who are here today will be here to speak ten years hence of what has taken place at this time. It was because of that and because of what must have impressed itself upon everyone who has been present during the past two weeks, that I thought it advisable to say that when the House of Commons was again confronted with the question of redistribution of the constituencies of Canada, it would in my opinion be wise for it to adopt the plan of referring the whole matter to a commission composed of judges-
Et cetera, et cetera. And he concludes:
That is the position which I took this afternoon and which I take again tonight.
And the next morning apparently the right hon. gentleman had forgotten all about that position which he had taken.
In those quotations which I have placed on the .record, Mr. Chairman, I think I have said enough to show the difference between Philip drunk and Philip sober; I think I have said enough to show the difference between the present Prime Minister's protestations of virtue and his actions; I think I have said enough to show the difference between his position when he is in opposition and when he is in power; indeed:, I think I have said enough to show the absolute worthlessness of Liberal promises.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
During the budget debate I said a few words concerning redistribution of electoral divisions. Nobody is more anxious than I am to have Quebec assume a greater influence in the House of Commons, but this influence should be based on equity, justice and right. I will not tolerate that Laval-Two Mountains be suppressed from the electoral map through the use of false excuses. Consequently I wish to denounce right now the shameful attitude of those who are endeavouring to proceed with redistribution in defiance of the importance of the population, history, geographical position and individual character of the county of Laval-Two Mountains.
This problem is nothing but an electoral scheme. They would not be worthy of sitting in this house who would take advantage of a redistribution of such national importance to satisfj: their mean ambitions or protect the interests of a political party, even if it is the party in power. I now quote figures which are more eloquent than the best speeches. According to the 1941 census Laval-Two Mountains had a population of 38,498. Glengarry, which is represented by the right hon. Prime Minister,

Redistribution
had a population of only 18,000; Vaudreuil-Soulanges had a population of 22.498, which is exactly 11,000 less than that of Laval-Two Mountains. Chateauguay-Huhtingdion, Stan-stead, Wright, Dorchester, Levis and Shefford, not to mention any others, all have populations less than that of Laval-Two Mountains; 25.339 ; 27.972; 28,771; 29,773; 30.411 and 33,387 respectively. When it is alleged, that the population of Laval-Two Mountains is insufficient, such an argument can be termed ridiculous and a pure fabrication. On several instances I have protested against this division of Laval-Two Mountains. In proof thereof I read the following letter which I received) on May 1, 1947, from the hon. member for Quebec South, who is chairman of the committee on redistribution:
Ottawa, May 1, 1947. Mr. Liguori Lacombe, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Colleague:
I beg to acknowledge your letter of April 30, to which you annexed a resolution passed by the municipality of the parish of St. Augustin, county of Two Mountains, together with copy of a protest against the dismemberment of Laval-Two Mountains, which protest was signed at Ste. Scholastique by Mr. Albert Laframboise, mayor of Ste. Scholasitique and president of the Catholic farmers' union for the district of Montreal, and by Mr. J. O. Latour, notary public at St. Benoit.
I see that, on several instances, you gave the subcommittee on redistribution for the province of Quebec, the reasons in favour of maintaining the status quo.
I remain,
Yours very truly,
(Signed) Charles G. Power.
Every day I receive from municipal councils in my own riding, resolutions requesting that Laval-Two Mountains be not dismembered. I have sent copies of each of these resolutions to the hon. members for Quebec South and for Outremont; the latter, as you know, is the chairman of the subcommittee on redistribution for the province of Quebec. Under the circumstances, the committee cannot claim that they are unaware of the facts and of the case.
There is another point I would, like to explain. The great majority of the population of l'He Jesus, which is a. portion of Laval-Two Mountains, is made up of farmers and gardeners. If you annex Pile Jesus to Montreal, you are annexing a farming district to industrial areas. I do not need to add that the interests of the producers and: of the consumers are not the same. During my political career, which covers quite a few years, I have come to realize quite often that the interests of producers and consumers are
radically opposed. It would have been quite easy for the committee to accept my representations and maintain the riding of Laval-Two Mountains in its true character. I know that my constituents will disapprove the changes which have thus been effected.
As to Argenteuil, there was a good reason why it should not have been changed. In that riding there is an important Englishspeaking minority ranging from 37 to 39 per cent of the total population. Why should the representation of minorities in the House of Commons be established in such a way that it loses its representative character? Minorities are entitled to be represented in the House of Commons. They pay taxes of all kinds, to the same extent as the majority. The action of the committee concerning the riding of Argenteuil and its English-speaking minority is exceedingly regrettable. This is a very serious wrong against this minority which deserves a better treatment. Furthermore, it creates a dangerous precedent. If the same treatment should be applied to present minorities in every province of this country, French-Canadians would revert to the position they occupied one hundred years ago in the history of Canada. We would have tc do once more everything we did to conquer and defend our rights. Anybody with a sense of justice and equity would approve what I am saying. Those who framed this infringement upon the rights of the English-speaking minority of Argenteuil will have to bear the responsibility of this action. Since I was elected to this house I have always defended the minority rights in Canada. I am still doing it for the sake of liberty, justice and equity. In the name of these great principles, Canada mobilized all of its resources. We are now witnessing the denial of the very rights of minorities in Argenteuil. I know the constituents of Argenteuil as well as those of Laval-Two Mountains. I have met them quite often in public meetings. I have the greatest respect and most sincere admiration for this population, whatever be their racial origin or their religious creed. For this reason, I know that these people will be deeply upset by the changes which are being effected in the federal representation without respecting the rights of an important part of its population. The population of Laval will resent deeply being separated from the population of Two Mountains to which it has been attached by economic and political ties for thirty years. I know that I am expressing the feelings of the people of Laval-Two Mountains as well as those of Argenteuil, which riding is adjacent to my riding and with which I am equally familiar.
Redistribution

In, participating in this debate I have the satisfaction of defending to the last the rights of my constituents to be justly and equitably represented in the Canadian parliament. So far as Laval-Two Mountains is concerned this redistribution is a masterpiece of disloyalty and unfairness. Some will claim that this redistribution is based upon papulation and geographical location, but it will take a great-deal of impertinence to put forth such an argument.
The population of Laval-Two Mountains exceeds 33,000. The population of Vaudreuil-
Soulanges is at least 10.000 less than the population of my riding, which exceeds by exactly 15,000 the population of Glengarry. Argenteuil has as large a population as Vaudreuil-Soulanges and Glengarry, and Laval-Two Mountains is much more populous than the two counties I have mentioned.
This is simply a prextext to get rid of a member who many times has been the object of similar and unsuccessful attacks on the part of the Liberal party. This is the same Liberal party which I defended most sincerely for more than twenty-five years. Forty years have gone by since the general election of 1917 when I endorsed the candidacy of my predecessor in this House of Commons who was a member without interruption from 1896 until 1925. I became his successor in the House of Commons on October 29, 1925, and I am still here. It will take more than this unfair deed to get rid of me. My good friends-of the committee will have me visiting in their constituencies at the next general election.

speechtext:
The letter reads as
follows:
House of Commons, Canada,
Ottawa, April 2, 1947. Mr. Liguori Laeombe, M.P.,
Ste, Scholastique, P.Q.
My dear Colleague:
After you left yesterday, I thought of suggesting to you that, after this recess-
Referring to the Easter recess.
-when Hartt is introduced in the chamber, this would be a proper occasion for you to cross the floor.
May I suggest that you prepare for the newspapers a statement about communism and the dangers of numerous parties-
That is the C.C.F. and other parties.

which can only benefit the Conservative party, which party the great majority of French Canadians do not want to see leading the government.
The more I think about this, the more I am convinced it will be to your future advantage.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Who signed it?

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: H. E. Brunelle, member for Champlain, on the redistribution committee. This is the scandal of the Liberal party.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: A big one.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Yes, it is a great scandal. I will produce in a few moments, Mr. Chairman, a photostat copy of the letter in French sent to me by the member for Champlain. I wish to denounce this shameful bargaining.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Who is bargaining?

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
This is bargaining. He offered not to touch my county if I crossed the floor, and I refused. I do not want to be interrupted. I want forty minutes or more than forty minutes to make my speech.
I wish to denounce this shameful bargaining, together with the business of this blackmail.
I shall never give in to this disgrace. I have been on this side of the house for five years because I am certain of my principles. I am a member of the House of Commons, and if I run again I will still be a member as long as Providence gives me health and strength to protect myself against traps which are set for me. Some people like the hon. member for Portneuf tried to do away with me at the general elections of 1940 and 1945. But I am here in the House of Commons and I will remain here whenever I choose to run, because my compatriots are grateful, loyal and proud.
I would draw to the attention of the committee and of the hon. member for Champlain standing order 7S of this house, which reads as follows:
'The offer of any money or other advantage to any member of this house, for the promoting ot any matter whatsoever depending or to be transacted in parliament, is a high crime and misdemeanour, and tends to the subversion ot the constitution.
Many persons make it the aim of their lives to upset the constitution of this country. Where will this lead them to ? M hat do scoundrels and fanatics of every kind intend to do with our tottering democracy? It is easy to solve this problem. I am not interested in the plots of those who amend the constitution of this country for the very purpose of further transgressing it. Nobody will believe that the best way of increasing the influence of the province of Quebec in the House of Commons is by acting in a way contrary to justice and equity. You cannot create eight new constituencies by suppressing, in contempt of freedom, justice and right, a county whose population, seniority, geographical position, and individual character and aspect entitle and authorize it to remain what it is and what it always was.
With this explanation of the reasons why Laval-Two Mountains should retain its status quo, I believe I have performed my duty towards my constituents. I sincerely hope that enlightenment will prevail in order that the authors of this error be not subjected to the condemnation of every honest person in this country.
Ri'ilistribution

I have only one thing in this world, the most precious of all, my honour. I will defend it against every attack from all sides. I spurn with contempt this groundless insult which is thrown at my constituents, because its origin is too low to reach their dignity and their honour. These conspirators will be crushed under the weight of their ignominy. If they perform this vile deed, they will go down into history as prominent robbers. They stole from Laval-Two Mountains its true character, its history, even its glorious name. The populace will point them out and say: Here are the conspirators of the year 1947 who are going into oblivion. Since everything dies, disappears and fades away in this world, they have nothing to fear since they are already dead in the mind and memory of their compatriots.
Here is part of an editorial in Le Canada, dated April 28, 1947:
At the end of his career, Mackenzie King, this foremost Canadian, while taking a solitary walk in this ancient city of Virginia, must have remembered his grandfather, William Lyon Mackenzie, who with Louis Joseph Papineau, was the father of democracy.
This is why I am requesting the Prime Minister, in memory of his ancestor's struggles towards the establishing of a government responsible to the Canadian people and towards democracy, to prevent this foul deed concerning the riding I am representing. This is the constituency where the ancestors of responsible government and Canadian democracy fulfilled a magnificent duty towards the country. The glorious history of Laval-Two Mountains must not be struck off with a stroke of the pen. In the name of truth, equity and justice, the Prime Minister must see to it that this shameful deed be not performed.
Before ending this speech, I would like to answer the remarks of the hon. member for Outremont addressed to me in a letter on May 29, 1947. I am sure the hon. member has a copy of the letter; I have not. The hon. member claims that it is impossible to increase the division of Vaudreuil-Soulanges whose population is less than that of Laval-Two Mountains by exactly 11,000 persons. To support his contention, he states that the boundaries of VaudTeuil-Soulanges are, on one side, the limits of the province of Ontario and, on the other two sides, the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa rivers. And what are the boundaries of Vaudreuil-Soulanges on the fourth side?
The hon. member is a very clever lawyer.
1 cannot believe he forgot that Vaudreuil-Soulanges has four boundaries. But, for his purpose, he forgot that the riding of Jacques-
Cartier is also adjacent to Vaudreuil-Soulanges. He made no bones about throwing in 1 'lie Jesus beyond the river des Prairies or Back river. As chairman of the subcommittee of the province of Quebec, the hon. member, if he had repressed his scruples, could have suggested that Vaudreuil-Soulanges be enlarged at the expense of Jacques-Cartier. And thus his first excuse is null.
Let us examine the second one. In the same letter, the hon. member claims that there was a substantial increase in the population of the ridings I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks. I quite agree with that. But the same applies to Laval-Two Mountains. And the hon. member is well aware of these facts. During the last ten years, the agricultural and labour population of Laval-Two Mountains has increased to a considerable extent.
In short, I lay the fate of Laval-Two Mountains in the hands of the hon. members of this house, for whom, as goes an old French saying, "success means nothing; but duty ' before all."
I cannot end these remarks without paying tribute to the memory of a man for whom I had great admiration. His stirring eloquence, his deep culture, were often responsible for the victories won by the party in power. Several times he was a minister in the federal cabinet. In the full bloom of his admirable career he was torn away from the admiration in which he was held by his city of Montreal, over whose destiny he presided as first magistrate. I do not know why it was in this very chamber that the most meagre tributes were paid to his memory, this chamber which he honoured with all the magnificence of his brilliant 'eloquence.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
History will vindicate his memory from the conspiracy of silence which was planted over his grave. Fernand Rinfret was a statesman in the fullest meaning of the word. Because he was a man of sincerity and honour, he never would have permitted this unfair deed towards Laval-Two Mountains. He was my friend, and during every election campaign I was fighting for him in St. James, Montreal. Who will give us men like Fernand

Redistribution
Rinfret? The hon. member for Outremont bears a great name. I ask him not to tie this name to this infamous bill whose only purpose is to delete from the electoral map the division of Laval-Deux Montagnes, where the builders of responsible government died sword in hand so their country could be great and immortal.
Finally, to excuse their attitude, some will say: A Liberal member, in this redistribution, is also losing his constituency. Nobody will be led to believe that a prejudice can be rectified by adopting an act of injustice.
After all, the attitude of the member for Champlain, as a member of the committee on redistribution and appointed to such committee by the government, can be termed the greatest scandal of the present administration. Before the people of Canada, the government must bear the serious responsibility of such an act.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
The introduction of this bill proves the truth of an old saying, that there is nothing new under the sun. Bills of this sort have been introduced before, some in this house and some elsewhere. I have been looking for precedents and I find one almost on all fours with the present bill. It is found in the well-known book by Lewis Carroll, Alice in Wonderland, at page 85. I hope the house will bear with me a moment while I quote from this well-known law book :
And the queen said, "Call hither the Lord High Chamberlain, for I would speak with him.''
And the Lord High Chamberlain, having been summonsed said, "At your service, Your Majesty!"
Said the queen:	"I have been greatly distressed by the reports from some electoral constituencies in this fair domain, namely Mus-kokas, Central Waters, Pawneepa, Kaloopus and Mount Laval. It would seem that there have appeared in these constituencies, certain men of intelligence and fortitude, leaders in their communities. who, unfortunately for me, are gifted with wisdom and speech, and who claim to be versed in the principles of a cult known as "democracy," under -which they claim the right to speak against my authority to rule this domain. My Lord High Chamberlain, will you please accept my order to take these disturbing subjects out and chop off their heads."
Lord High Chamberlain:	"Do I understand
Your Majesty to instruct me to chop off all their heads?"
Her Majesty:	"All their heads."
And the Lord High Chamberlain, having retired from the queen's court, returned in an hour's time.
Lord High Chamberlain:	"Your Majesty, I
have rounded up the members of Muskokas. Central Waters. Pawneepa. Kaloopus and Mount Laval, and I have taken them out and chopped off their heads."
Her Majesty:	"Are their heads all chopped
off?"
Lord High Chamberlain:	Yes, Your Majesty,
their heads are all chopped off."
I know that the house will agree with me that this was a very sad incident, but the precedent is apt.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
