speechtext:
The only difficulty is that Alice woke up.
Mr. J. M. MACDONNELL OMuskoka-Ontario): It is only suitable that the intended victims should be heard from. Like tlhe member for Winnipeg North, I am sorry that the Prime Minister is not in his seat-not because we would salute him, like the victims in the crena of old, saying "We who are about to die salute thee", for we do not propose to die. But it would have been nice to have him here particularly because, like the member for Winnipeg North, I propose to quote from him also and to quote somewhat freely. I should think the Prime Minister would be highly flattered with the extent to which we on this side find it convenient to quote him, and it is surprising the number of wise things he seems to have said in the past.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: That was long ago.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
It would be hypocrisy for anyone to pretend that he does not feel deeply aggrieved when he finds that he is to be turned into a kind of stranger and sojourner in the land, and certainly after the labour of winning a constituency one feels very badly that it is being suddenly dismembered. You cannot do the work which is necessary in order to win a constituency without making a great many friends, and however high your hopes may be that you can find some other dwelling place and come back here in spite of all, nevertheless [DOT] you feel very badly at the thought of losing friends or the thought of being separated from them, whatever the final result may be.
However I am not proposing today to spend much time talking about my own woes. One of the reasons is that I doubt very much whether I shall wring very many tears from hon. gentlemen opposite by talking about my woes. I imagine they have discounted these feelings in advance and therefore I will not discuss them.
I do, however, wish to talk about my own constituency. In my first speech I pointed out that we are here only because our constituents cannot be here. We are here representing them and I believe that in what I say I shall be representing them. At any rate I shall try to.
Redistribution

What do they think of all this? I have been up there and I have heard from a number of them and so far as I can find out there is a surprising unanimity that they do not like being pushed around in this way. They will like it still less, I hope, when they have read what I have had to say, and which I propose to send them, because if I have the least bit of success in what I say, they will feel that this is an arbitrary, unreasonable, unreasoning and, I might say, preposterous thing that is being done. I cannot find a reason for it, and if I am successful they also will feel that there is no reason for it.
I do not in this matter represent wholly and exclusively my own riding of Muskoka. The people of Parry Sound, I may say, do not like this and I have had the honour of receiving communications from one or two of them. Of course, I have received communications by the hundred from my own constituents and many communications from town councils, municipal councils and various organizations of that kind. I wish to read one communication from Parry Sound, partly because it is very short, partly because it is direct, and partly because it is from the Parry Sound Liberal Association. It is addressed to me, and by the way, they say:
You are at perfect liberty to use this as you wish in your endeavour to maintain the present standing of the ridings.
This is what they say:
In connection with the proposal of the committee on redistribution, in the matter of the electoral ridings of Muskoka and Parry Sound districts, I wish to state that we wish to protest against their action, and regard it as unfair, unjust and an infringement on the rights and liberties of the good people who go to make up these two grand old ridings of Muskoka and Parry Sound districts.
This is signed' by D. F. Quinlan, president of the Parry Sound' District Liberal Association. I was glad to receive that, because it will supply some evidence of what I believe to be the fact, that a large number of people, utterly regardless of party, will dislike thus being pushed around'. I can see no reason why this should be done. They are being dealt round like a pack of cards, and I shall have something to say about that in a few minutes.
I have one more word to say about myself.
I seem to be in good' company, because apparently there are some other people who have worked for this party and done their best and who will be kept out of this house, if it, is possible to have that done. I do not know whether we should flatter ourselves that it is thought desirable to pin us down as much as possible. We are constantly assured that 
the government is confident that nothing can shake it. I do not think this will be regarded as exhibit A for that confidence.
I am glad to have received these communications from Parry Sound, because after this redistribution goes through I hope I may be fortunate enough to get the nomination in. the new riding. I shall try to get it and if I do get it I believe that I and my good; friend, who is not in his seat today, will be able to carry on the election in a decent and sporting manner, though I am glad the contest is not to carried out on the ice.
I thought it was best in this matter to try to find some principles which might guide and which might be of interest. Certainly they are of interest to me. I thought it well, as far as possible, not to quote anyone who might be regarded as in any way prejudiced in favour of the party to which I happen to belong. I have been fortunate in finding some interesting quotations laying down, as I think, sound principles, from Sir Wilfrid Laurier and also the present Prime Minister. First I should like to quote from Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Speaking in this house on February 17, 1914, in a redistribution debate, he quotes with approval words which he himself had used in an earlier debate in 1892. Here are the words:
But I fully recognize that in such a measure the guiding principle should be as far as possible to equalize the population in all the constituencies.
He quotes that from 1892 and adds, "I have nothing to retract of those words." He is careful later on in his speech to point out that you cannot have absolute arithmetical equality. I want to read this part because I think it is important; it also points out at any rate one of the great qualifications of arithmetic equality. Sir Wilfrid said, as reported at page 847 of Hansard of February 17, 1914:
Without going into all the reasons, there is one supreme reason, namely, that in a country like Canada, where there is a very large territory with a sparse population, if you were to give the same unit of population to cities and counties, in rural constituencies you would have such a large area of territory as to he almost impossible to control or to cover. This is quite sufficient to justify the principle which has been adopted on^every occasion on which we have had redistribution.
The second principle which Sir Wilfrid lays down happens to be important on this occasion, because, as I see it, this riding of mine has been dealt around like a pack of cards. Sir Wilfrid says this, as reported at page 845 of Hansard:
There is another principle of almost equal importance, and that is regard for the compactness of the constituency, and, as far as possible,

Redistribution
for the county unit. Under our system, the county is the unit of population, so far as public life is concerned.
Later, on the same page, he said this:
It seems to me obvious that if you interfere with the lines of the county units, separate those who meet periodically for the discharge of their municipal and other duties, and provide that they shall only meet once in four or five years to decide on political questions, you detract from,- rather than add to, their appreciation of public questions.
In my opinion that statement by Sir Wilfrid Laurier was an extremely wise one, and I believe that anyone, even one who has had as little experience in country ridings as I have had, will have been greatly struck by the fact that the people you run into who are interested in politics are almost to a man those who have taken part, in municipal associations. I was interested in making a rough calculation and I came to the conclusion that in a country riding like mine there are somewhere between one hundred and two hundred times as many people taking an active part in self-government as there are in a large city. I believe if anyone works that out he will find it is nearer two hundred than one hundred. That is why I think Sir Wilfrid Laurier was on sound ground when he said that you take these people who are engaged in political life in their own county and you try as far as possible to maintain that principle when you are making constituencies.
The third principle that I want to quote was laid down by the present Prime Minister on May 23, 1933, when he was leader of the opposition. He says this as reported at page 5238 of Hansard'.
And may I say with respect to a question like the redistribution of seats in the House of Commons, on which the whole basis of government itself rests, that this parliament is not merely exercising its function of legislating, it is exercising the function of the high court of parliament wherein it is expected to see that justice is done to all electors in the country, those who may not be in a position to represent their own views except by the members who happen to be representing them in particular constituencies at this time, as well as those who speak through their members. I submit that there is no higher trust imposed upon a House of Commons under our constitution than that of justly redistributing the constituencies. That trust is one which must be exercised not alone in the light of what is in the interest of the sitting member or the constituency he represents, but in a wholly or impartial and broadminded way in the light of what is most just and fair to the great body of the electorate.
I should like to quote just one further passage from the Prime Minister later in the debate where he raised the question of the previous redistribution. That was in the
twenties, when he was Prime Minister, and when there was some question with regard to his then constituency of North York. The Prime Minister has been around quite a bit since then.

speechtext:
Speaking here, he says as reported at page 5279:
I took the position that as Prime Minister I was not going to ask any favours for myself, or expect for the constituency I represented, anything which I would not ask equally for any other constituency.
I am particularly sorry that the Prime Minister is not here to hear that, and I hope that some good angel will see to it that he reads that part of my speech, if no other.
AVe have three principles laid down there by Sir AVilfrid Laurier and by the present Prime Minister. The first is the substantial equality of members, subject to what Sir Wilfrid pointed out as to the difference between city and country; the second is adherence to municipal and county boundaries, and the third is justice to all the electors. I have been careful to take those principles from authorities which I am sure the government will not question.
If we accept those principles, let me apply them to my constituency of Muskoka-Ontario. I can be brief on this, because the argument, I think, is not hard to make. Muskoka-Ontario has a population of just a little over
35,000.	It is large for a country riding. When this redistribution came up I felt absolutely invulnerable, because I thought it was too large to be regarded as a small riding and on the other hand was too small to be regarded as a huge riding. I thought I was on safe middle ground. Therefore I was incredulous when I first heard of the suggestion which was made. I thought that some enemy of mine must have suggested it. I now know that he was not an enemy but was merely a well-informed man. I should like to make two points here, and I think they are both important. A good deal will be said later on about averages, and I just want to make one point. My constituency of Muskoka-Ontario has a population of 35,000. There are nineteen Ontario ridings with a population of under 30,000, and the smallest, of course- and I mention this rather hesitantly; I wish the Prime Minister were here to hear it-is Glengarry7, which heads or tails the list, whichever you like, with a population of 18,732.
Redistribution

I make one further comment on that. A little mental arithmetic will have shown hon. gentlemen already that my constituency as it stands is approximately twice the size, in the matter of population, of the Prime Minister's; but the new constituency which is to be set up-and for which I hope, with good luck, to get the nomination-will have some 51,000 of population, or approximately three times that of Glengarry. I submit that the figures I have given show that this proposal to wipe out or butcher the constituency of Muskoka-Ontario disregards in the most flagrant manner every one of those three principles which I have quoted from authorities which will be accepted. Let me recall to your mind, Mr. Chairman, what they were: First, substantial equality, as. explained by Sir Wilfrid; second, adherence to municipal and county boundaries. There I should digress for a moment. As I said a few minutes ago, the riding is being dealt around like a pack of cards. There are six townships in the Ontario part of that riding. Two of those are being attached to southern Ontario, and they do not much like that because they feel they are just an appanage to the city of Oshawa, which now dominates that riding. Four are being tossed over into the next county, Victoria. Then you come to Muskoka. Part of it, as the Secretary of State explained earlier, is being cut off and thrown across to North Simcoe, I think it is. The balance, truncated in that way, is to be attached to the district of Parry Sound. That is what it being done. As I say, they are reduced to bits and pieces, thrown all over the map; and I don't believe they like it.
I submit that I have made out something in the nature of what the lawyers would call a prima facie case; but against this you will naturally say there must be some arguments for it or it would not have been done. Quite true; and I am coming now to the arguments for it. The chairman of the subcommittee was kind enough to give me a memorandum. I doubt very much if the hon. member for Grey-Bruce was very happy about this thing;
I doubt very much if he felt entirely convinced about his memorandum, but however that may be he gave me a memorandum from which I now propose to quote. The first reason, quoting from his memorandum which I have here, is this:
Some of us decided on Muskoka-Ontario simply because it was nearest geographically to what is generally referred to as the north-
That is the northern area. There are two reasons in one here, really:
-and on the ground that the unit of representation of Parry Sound would be almost the same as the average of the north constituencies. 
I submit that those two reasons, as they say somewhere in Gilbert and Sullivan, like the flowers that bloom in the spring have nothing to do with the case. What possible bearing on the question of redistribution or on the wiping out of my constituency has the fact that it happens to be near the northern constituencies? I cannot see it. If you look at a map you see that Muskoka-Ontario is near the northern counties, but what earthly reason is that for suggesting that regardless of population and regardless of all the considerations which must be taken into account you can pick on this constituency, merely because it happens geographically to be near some others? I say that has nothing whatever to do with it.
The second part of the reason is that Parry Sound will have almost the same average population as the northern constituencies. What has that to do with it? Why pick out the northern constituencies? Why not pick out the southern ones, or the western ones, or the eastern ones? Why not remember Glengarry? Why not remember, too, that there are nineteen ridings in Ontario with populations of less than 30,000, while the population of my present riding is 35,000. I doubt very much that the hon. member for Grey-Bruce was very happy with the first reason, and I doubt if he was even that happy with the second one. Here is the second reason:
Others considered Muskoka-Ontario to be a combination of diverse economic interests and subject to improvement.
Somebody said, "subject to political improvement." However, I am not going to try to be funny about it, because there is a point in that reason which I want to discuss. The point is the reference to a combination of diverse economic interests, and I think it very interesting that this reason should be given. The suggestion there, as far as I can make out, is that when a member comes down here he is a lobbyist, that he is just to represent the interests of his riding, that he has no broader duty and that therefore if possible you should give him just one interest to represent. I think this would be a most extraordinary place if we had here 245 people each feeling himself pledged to represent one interest. I say that would be the destruction of democratic government. I believe that reason is one of the most vicious and unsound reasons that could be given. Incidentally, and happily, I think the fact is that if you took stock of the ridings here you would find at least one hundred, I suspect one hundred and fifty and I hope even more members who on analysis would be found to represent a combination of diverse economic interests. I

Redistribution
hope that is true, because if it is true it is healthy, and if it is not true it is unhealthy. Therefore I say to me that reason is not only no reason, but it is in reverse, a reason for leaving the riding as it is.
The final reason is a rather complicated statement of the average population figures for ridings in central southern Ontario and eastern southern Ontario. I find this very complicated, and therefore am reading it. I can hardly understand it myself, and I am not sure I could state it without reading it. Beginning with the proposition that a seat must come from southern Ontario, the memorandum proceeds to argue on the basis of the figures given that it must be from central southern Ontario, in other words from a bloc of constituencies which includes Muskoka-Ontario. But that again entirely ignores the fact I have already pointed out, that this constituency of mine is much larger than nineteen other ridings in Ontario, all of which have less than 30,000 population, and many of them very much less. I have looked at some of the figures. Beginning, with Glengarry with 18,732, they show population of 21,000, 21,000,
22,000,	23,000, 25,000, and so on-much smaller than my riding.
Now I should like briefly to take stock of the situation. I have tried to glean some principles which seemed to me sound in dealing with this matter. I have taken them from recognized authorities; they seem to me wise. If I have not completely failed I have done something to persuade you that on these reasons there is no case whatever for the dismemberment of Muskoka-Ontario. As I said a little while ago, I am in good company; but that does not do anything to comfort me, and still less to comfort the people of my riding. As things are now we have the hon. member for Lake Centre, who is a special target and whose constituency has had such an amount of axe and shovel work done on it that I think it would take a combination of a civil engineer and a Philadelphia lawyer to find the boundaries. The hon. member for Vancouver South has already dealt with Kamloops and with the constituency at present represented by my leader. But I want to say one thing further, because naturally the question has arisen in one's mind as to what the Prime Minister has to say about all this. Again let me say I am sorry he is not here, because I am going to quote from him, and indeed discuss him a little in the few minutes I have remaining to me.
Before I forget I should like to say one thing. That is, there was one member of that committee, the hon. member for Quebec South, who seemed to me to show some spirit 83166-356
of fairness and sportsmanship in this business. I think he did not like this, and my understanding is that he tried to have it sent back but was overruled. I imagine there are other people who are more biddable than he, and who carry out the orders of the boss with greater complaisance. But now I am coming back to the Prime Minister. I have here a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of April 28. This was just after the right hon. gentleman had come back from the south, and I suppose he was full of the milk of human kindness. This clipping is headed, "Mr. King not pleased with changes in ridings". I propose to quote somewhat freely from this article. It begins by saying:
With the return of Prime Minister King to his office in Ottawa today, it is expected that a considerable number of recommendations recently made by the House of Commons redistribution committee will be turned back to Chairman C. G. Power and his associates for reconsideration. A source close to the Prime Minister told the Journal today that Mr. King is not altogether satisfied with the committee's reports and recommendations.

Politically speaking the constituency of Villeneuve is a really good one because it is a stronghold of the Union of Electors and Social Credit. But the idea which I have and which I hope we all have is not to regard this as a political question but as a matter of doing justice and right to>
the citizens of the whole country. A part of this new constituency, Temiscamingue which, is to be annexed to the southern part of the; present constituency of Pontiac, has already made known its wishes. asking that that area be annexed to the lower part of Pontiac. Prom the standpoint of geography, communications, and from the business point of view that is nonsense, because Temiseamingue naturally belongs to the northern part. They are dealing with Rouyn and Noranda all the time, and they have nothing to do with the lower part of Pontiac. If they want to go to lower Pontiac they cannot reach it by roads in their own constituency because they have no highway; they have nothing; they are obliged to go through North Bay or to go through Montreal to reach Shawville and Campbell's Bay. I met some people of Temiseamingue a couple of weeks ago and they asked me to tell the committee and the house that their desire and will is to be connected1 with Rouyn and Noranda and with the northern part of Pontiac. If there are any political ideas behind this division of the constituency of Pontiac I think the organizers certainly missed the point, because we can organize there just as well as anywhere else in Canada. The only thing I am asking for today is justice for the people of Temiseamingue who want to remain connected with the north. If we have too large a population in the north it is up to the committee or the house to divide the northern part in two, leaving lower Pontiac alone or annexing lower Pontiac to another riding in the south. Then all the people in the north will be satisfied. We want justice and nothing else.
I should like to say a few words about Laval-Two Mountains. I am one hundred per cent in favour of what the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains said this afternoon, it is certainly an injustice to him to have his constituency struck off completely. He is an old member of the house, but now that constituency is to lose its name and be annexed to another riding. I think that something should be done and could be done in this matter which would be to the advantage of the population. I am not looking at this matter simply from the point of view of the member who represents that constituency, but from the point of view of the will of the people of Laval-Two Mountains. Our obligation is to forget political considerations, and if some of the organizers are not pleased with the present set-up they have only to cross their fingers and wait until the election comes, when we will show them what the people of this country want. They want justice; they want their rights protected, and when the majority of the people have expressed their wishes the government should concern itself with the will of the people and should legislate accordingly.

I rise at this time to make a protest against the mutilation of the good old riding of Wentworth. I may say that I protested several months ago. I did not leave it until the dying hours of this session. I wrote to the editor of the Dundas Star on April 25. He published this letter in his issue of May 1, and it reads as follows:
Gordon Anslow, Esq.,
Editor, Dundas Star,
Dundas, Ontario Dear Mr. Editor:
The redistribution committee, predominantly representing this present government, are proposing to remove from Wentworth the townships of Beverly, Aneaster, Glanford and Bin-brook and are going to put them into a new constituency to be called Brant-Wentworth.
I have protested against it! I am protesting against it. and will have more to say about it when the bill appears in the house. Wentworth has not had its county boundaries broken in over forty-five years, and there is no good or sensible reason for doing it now. I object to being kicked around, and we are. It is just plain political skulduggery, and I have had and I am having no part of it. I am making that statement now at this first opportunity and am not waiting until the damage is done. Mind you, I am leaning backwards politically, as every one of those four townships returns a Liberal majority, but if I did not protest this move I would not be doing my duty to the good people of Wentworth. I am placing the matter right on the doorstep of the Liberal organization of Wenitworth riding and it is up ,to them. I am washing my hands of it. I will have none of it.

I have grave doubts whether the Liberal association of Wentworth were ever consulted aJbout the matter or knew much about it until the damage was done. On May 17 I received the following letter from the county clerk and treasurer of the county of Wentworth.
Dear Sir:	We are enclosing for your consideration a copy of a resolution passed unanimously at the recent session of Wentworth county council.
As the redistribution proposed at the present time involves the transfer to Brant riding of more than half the area of Wentworth county, it was strenuously opposed by all members of council.
By the way, I may say that about fifty per cent of the members of the county council of Wentworth are Liberals, the other fifty per cent being Progressive Conservatives. It was moved by councillor W. S. Milmine. seconded by councillor B. E. Corman:
That this council of the corporation of the county of Wentworth hereby records its disapproval of and protests against any redistribution of the federal ridings which may involve the transfer of portions of the federal riding of Wentworth to the Brant or any other federal riding, and
That a copy of this resolution be transmitted to the chairman of the redistribution committee of the House of Commons.
This resolution was passed on May 15, 1947, and forwarded on May 17. I am sure it will be of interest to the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris) the very fine chairman of the committee for Ontario, of which I have no criticism. I say it will be interesting for him to know that the motion was seconded by Mr. B. E. Corman, a brother of the former member for Wentworth, who is also a friend of mine. It seems strange that this should be seconded by Mr. Corman's brother.
In my opinion this thing started by putting the township of Burford in the constituency of Brantford City. The present hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald.) would have no objection to that, because Burford township has always returned a slight Liberal majority. But they take the remainder of Brant county and put it in that, constituency with four townships of Wentworth, to make it one of the most rambling constituencies of Ontario. To quote from the Dundas Star of May 1, 1947, this is what the editor, Mr. Anslow, says in part:
Residents of Wentworth are wondering where the equity of such a "redistribution" lies. They look at a map and wonder just where such matters may end. They consider that for generations they have voted in Wentworth and feel that at this stage in the constituency's history no change should be made-especially when it will not result in at least a better geographical division.

If these two new townships of Glanford and Binbrook were to be taken from the riding of Wentworth, the right and proper place to put them would be the constituency of Haldimand.
In conclusion, may I say that I do not consider that in a riding such as Wentworth the removal of one or two or three thousand of its population from the constituency means anything at all when the constituency is so large. But I say that in a riding which has been either Liberal or Conservative since confederation, the committee should consider seriously making this alteration, because I am giving fair warning now that, whether the candidate be Liberal or Progressive Conservative, he will have far fewer supporting votes to carry into the more congested area of the present riding of Wentworth to fight communism.

speechtext:
I will direct my remarks particularly to section 2 of the bill. The section adds to the federal district of Yukon that part of Mackenzie district west of the 109th meridian of west longitude, and the original bill added the whole of the Mackenzie district. The change to the 109th meridian of west longitude does not make much difference. It makes the boundary of the new constituency, if it becomes a constituency, as I hope it will not, that much more difficult to find. The east boundary before was the boundary of the district of Mackenzie. Now it is the 109th meridian of west longitude. How will anyone find that? It has not been surveyed or marked out, whereas the boundaries of Mackenzie district have been surveyed and marked out.
Why that change was made I do not know. Yukon has an area of 207,076 square miles and the Mackenzie district has an area of 527,490 square miles, a total of Mackenzie and Yukon, of 734,566 square miles.
The present section makes a constituency of over 700,000 square miles in area, if anyone can visualize that. It is unwieldy and so vast
that it is impossible. I hold up a map of Canada on which hon. members can see Yukon and the Mackenzie. The combined area will be larger than British Columbia and Alberta combined; larger than Alberta and Saskatchewan combined; larger than Saskatchewan and Manitoba; as large as Ontario and almost as large as Quebec and the maritimes. That, to me, is a monstrosity. Why anyone took the notion to make such a constituency I do not understand, but I will make a guess before I get through.
To begin with, Yukon and this district of Mackenzie are separated' by two high ranges of mountains. They have nothing whatever in common. Mackenzie district does all its business and all its trading with central Canada, with Edmonton for the most part. It would be much more appropriate to add the Mackenzie district to a northern constituency in Alberta or Saskatchewan than to Yukon to the west. Yukon does its trading with the west coast of Canada, with Vancouver, Victoria and Prince Rupert. The Mackenzie district does practically all its trading with Edmonton. We have nothing in common.
Does any member of the house feel thait he could reasonably represent such a constituency and get around it? Is he wealthy enough to own or charter a plane to go and visit the people in his constituency from time to time, as he should? And not only in an election. In an election it will cost a fortune, and it will cost the government of Canada a great deal of money to carry on an election there. As evidence of that, they have already increased the chief electoral officer's pay by $2,000, because of the additional expense he would be put to in such a condition.
What is the population? At the last census the Yukon population of white people was only 3,174, and of Mackenzie district was 2,113, a total of 5,287. I estimate that today- and I am in a position to make a fair estimate-there are not 10,000 included in the two districts. Some people say that this is mandatory on the part of this parliament. We need only to look at the section of the British North America Act as amended to convince ourselves that it is not mandatory. Section 51 (2) reads as follows:
The Yukon territory as constituted by chapter 41 of the Statutes of Canada (1991), together with any part of Canada not comprised within a province which may from time to time-
Redistribution

And note those words "may from time to time".
-be included therein by the parliament of Canada for the purpose of representation in parliament, shall be entitled to one member.
The parliament of Canada may or may not, just as it chooses. It does not have to do anything of the kind, and I say that it should not. Other people will say that they do not wish to disfranchise the people of the Mackenzie district. The bulk of the people of the Mackenzie district live at the new and coming mining camp of Yellowknife. That is a splendid gold mining camp which is bound to grow and will produce wonderful wealth. They have not a population of 5,000. The rest of the people in the Mackenzie district are but a few hundreds who live away up miles north of Great Bear lake where uranium is being produced. If this bill is not passed1 adding that part of Mackenzie district to Yukon, these people are not disfranchised. They are left as they are, and that is what they asked parliament to do. They have done that by telegram from their board of trustees. They have done it by petition and in every other way. They d'o not want the franchise on the terms of this bill and I do not see why parliament should insist on giving it to them. Back in 1930 there was before this house a bill, which happened to be Bill No. 13, an unlucky number. By that bill it was intended to add the whole of the northwest territories to Yukon and make one electoral constituency; in other words, that constituency would have been extended from Alaska on the west to the Atlantic ocean on the east and to the north pole on the north. It was so ridiculous that parliament would not listen to it and they dropped the bill. When I discussed this matter in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I said1, as reported at page 695 of Hansard:
I cannot better describe the section of the bill to which I have referred than to say that it is outrageous legislation, the iniquity of which could not be overstated. That portion of the bill seeking to form one constituency out of Yukon and the Mackenzie district is a legislative abortion.
I was followed in that debate by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who said:
May I just say a word in support of the grievance the previous speaker has presented to the house. When this matter was up for discussion at the time we had before us the resolution to Westminster asking for amendment to the British North America Act, hon. members of this group pointed out at that time how unfair it was to make one constituency across the whole of the North American continent, as the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) has just described it.

That is how that group felt about it. As long ago as March 10, I said, 'as reported at page 1209 of Hansard:
I predict that before the legislation becomes law, in its present atrocious form-and it is in an atrocious form-the people in the Mackenzie district themselves will protest, and will not submit to being so ruthlessly pushed around. I believe they would prefer to remain unrepresented in parliament rather than have to accept representation on the fantastically ridiculous terms proposed. There has scarcely been time to hear from them, but I predict we shall.
And we have. This is what came in from Yellowknife on March 15, 1945. It is a telegram addressed to the Secretary of State who, in the absence of the Prime Minister, was handling the bill, and reads as follows:
Yellowknife district miners union opposed to amalgamation of Yukon Mackenzie districts for electoral purposes. We demand that Mackenzie district be given separate electoral status.
Then the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), observing that they had not gone so far as to say that they did not want representation at all on those terms, had a telegram sen't to them; and a telegram came back to the effect that they preferred' to remain without representation rather than be joined to Yukon. They put the miners' union on record to that extent. The chairman of the committee will bear me out in that. Then there is another telegram to the Secretary of State, which reads as follows:
We the undersigned members of the local board of trustees of Yellowknife administrative district protest against proposed joint representation in parliament of Yukon and Mackenzie districts for the following reasons. No intercommunication between the two districts, no common interests among the people in the two districts, no desire by the people of either territory for joint representation. Financially impossible for one representative to serve both districts. Consensus of opinion would prefer no representative at present to proposed joint representation.
When that telegram was presented to the committee, what did the hon. member for Ottawa West say. The report in the Globe and Mail on March 26, in connection with the proceedings of the committee, reads, in part, as follows:
G. J. Mcllraith (Lib., Ottawa West) just couldn't believe that any five men would send such a message. He pointed to a statement in the Yellowknife telegram that it was "financially impossible" for any man to represent the widely separated Yukon and Northwest Territories. How, he asked, did the Yellowknife trustees know for certain that Canada had not a solitary citizen financially able to afford to sit as M.P. for both districts?

Redistribution
He may be financially able, but I am not; and I doubt if ninety-five per cent of the members of this house are financially able to represent that district as it should be represented.
So much for finances. Then I have a telegram addressed to the Prime Minister, from Yellowknife:
At open public mass meeting called by Northwest Territories association and representing all parties and shades of opinion the following resolution was passed unanimously:
"This meeting is bitterly opposed to amalgamation of the district of Mackenzie with Yukon Territory as an electoral constituency and demands the immediate creation of a constituency for the Mackenzie district under the provisions of the British North America Act, 1886."
Exhaustive canvass of public opinion fails to disclose even one supporter of proposed electoral amalgamation. Objections cite preposterously unwieldy size of proposed constituency, absolute lack of community or economic interest or of direct intercommunication between the two areas.
That is signed by John Murray McMeekan, president of the Northwest Territories association. The previous telegram was signed, among others, by Mr. J. G. McNiven, who is the first citizen of Canada other than a civil servant to have been appointed to the council of the Northwest Territories. I asked him if his appointment to that council would in any way handicap his opposition to the union of these two districts, and he replied, "No. If anything my objection ought to have more weight as coming from a member of that council." Then on April 22 he sent me the following telegram:
Received following wire from Murphy. "Wrote you today. One hundred per cent citizens against amalgamation. Petitions being signed and will be rushed to Black this week. Citizens here prepared wait two years, I would estimate." Will advise you further.
Then Mr. McNiven wrote me from Toronto on April 23:
For your information I am enclosing copy of letter addressed to the Honourable J. A. Glen. You will note that Mr. Murphy is keeping his promise to do everything to get representative petitions in Ottawa at the earliest possible date.
This is what Mr. McNiven wrote the Minister of Mines and Resources on April 23, 1947:
Following our conversation on Tuesday, April 15, re proposed merger of Yellowknife and Yukon districts, I wrote to Yellowknife to ascertain the popular feeling there and have received a reply from Mr. G. D. Murphy which reads in part as follows:
"For your information and Mr. Glen's this will advise you that the Hon. George Black visited this town last week and interviewed many people, under the writer's guidance, and 83166-357
one evening held a public meeting. No one here that met him or that was at the meeting was in favour of the present arrangement, viz: union for electoral purposes of the Yukon district and the Mackenzie. They, these people, all preferred to wait until such time as we were able to have our own representative in the federal house. He said he thought petitions circulated and signed by the people would be much more important to the committee in making its decision than wires from organizations, and acocrdingly we are now in the process of getting these signed. They will be sent to George Black via air mail this coming week and will be presented to the committee and quite possibly be produced on the floor of the house."
You will note that this definitely substantiates my own opinion in the matter, and I hope you will take the necessary delaying action to await the receipt of the petitions mentioned in this letter. You will recall meeting Mr. Murphy on your Yellowknife visit last year as president of the local board of trade. I personally have a great deal of faith in his judgment on matters of this nature and recommend him highly to you in the same capacity.
As I understand it, this matter started in this way. Last summer the Minister of Mines and Resources made a trip to Yellowknife by plane, and they suggested to him that they should have representation in parliament, to which he quite agreed. But they never expected that their representation in parliament would be brought about by adding most of the Mackenzie district to Yukon, and they were disappointed and surprised when they found this was the outcome of their interview with the minister. As I see it-and I am sure hon. members will say I am right-it would be just as appropriate to add the Mackenzie district to Nova Scotia as to add it to Yukon. It is just as easy to get from Nova Scotia to Mackenzie as to get from Yukon to Mackenzie. It would be just as appropriate to add Mackenzie to Glengarry as to add it to Yukon. This is the petition that came in from the people of Yukon:
That parliament is now considering Bill No. 18 which if enacted will be "The Representation Act 1947".
That it is proposed by said legislation to include with Yukon electoral district the said district of Mackenzie and the electoral district so created shall elect one member of the House of Commons.
That in the opinion of your petitioners it is not desirable to include the district of Mackenzie with the electoral district of Yukon for the reason that it will create a constituency of the enormous area of over seven hundred thousand square miles in extent, unwieldy and impracticable in every respect.
That Yukon territory and the district of Mackenzie have nothing in common, no community interest of any sort. They are separated by ranges of mountains, have no direct intercommunication, are entirely foreign to each other.

Your petitioners therefore pray that Mackenzie district be not included with the electoral district of Yukon. . . .
Now I have the petition from Mackenzie, with the same preamble:
That in the opinion of your petitioners it is not desirable to include the district of Mackenzie with the electoral district of Yukon for the reason that it will create a constituency of the enormous area of over seven hundred thousand square miles in extent, unwieldy and impracticable in every respect.
That Yukon territory and the district of Mackenzie have nothing in common, no community interest of any sort. They are separated by ranges of mountains, have no direct intercommunication, are entirely foreign to each other.
Remember, these are the people of Mackenzie.
That your petitioners prefer to have the representation of Mackenzie district to parliament postponed and to remain for the present without such representation rather than to have the district included with the electoral district of Yukon.
These are the wishes of the people of that district. Opposition to this legislation is unanimous in both Mackenzie and Yukon. Not one supporting voice has been found; no one has said, "Do it," and I challenge anyone who says there is support for this step to show where that support comes from. The people out there do not want it. They are the people who are affected. They have told you so in telegrams and petitions. Are you going to disregard their wishes? What good will this do? Why force it on them? Yellowknife is a coming mining camp; probably it will be one of the best Canada has ever seen. During the Easter holidays I made a trip there by plane just to find out how the people felt about the matter. We had a public meeting, and no one at that meeting was in favour of joining Mackenzie and Yukon. They asked me how they could influence parliament against it, and I advised them to send down petitions signed by as many of the people of that territory as they could get to sign. I told them that telegrams from organizations such as the board of trade and the board of trustees were all very well in their way, but that they did not represent the wide range of public opinion that petitions represented. They asked me if I would draw up the petitions, and those petitions were drafted by me at the request of those people.
I say this community of Yellowknife in the Mackenzie district should eventually have representation, but they do not want it now at this price. Eventually they will be entitled to representation, and I would be the last to put anything in the way of their getting it, but they do not want it this way and neither do I. They ask you not to do this atrocious

thing to them. I ask you on behalf of the people of Mackenzie and the people of Yukon not to do it. For my own sake it does not matter; it is neither here nor there, because this will probably be my last parliament. But I am thinking of the people who will come after me and who will be looking after the people in the great Yellowknife district and the people of Yukon.
As you know, or as you should know, Yukon has produced over $300 million worth of placer gold. They are now moving into hard rock gold mining, silver mining and lead mining. It is a coming camp just as the Yellowknife
is.	Eventually they should have representation in this parliament, but they do not want it at this price. Those who are best qualified say that they do not want it. I did not want to do it in this way; but, since the committee has decided that there will be a general discussion and the Secretary of State has moved an amendment to the clause in the schedule as to Nova Scotia, I would move:
That section 2 be amended by striking out the words, "including that part of the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories lying west of the 109th meridian of west longitude.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make with regard to what has happened in connection with the four York seats surrounding Toronto. When the census was taken I think the norm was 54,000 of population to one representative in this parliament. Since that time the number of seats in parliament has been increased1 so that the representation is somewhat less than 54,000. Because of difficulties of travel and for other reasons it is reasonable to expect that a rural seat should contain fewer population than an urban seat. A member representing a rural seat has to travel greater distances and has all the other difficulties inherent to representing a larger square mileage of territory.
However, the situation with regard to the Yorks goes far further than what I think could reasonably be expected. Let us assume that a reasonable proportion as between rural and urban representation in this house is sixty to forty; that is, an urban seat should have a population of some 60,000 and' a rural seat a population of some 40,000. There would, be some exceptions of course, but that would be the over-all picture. Let us see what happens with regard to the York seats. I am speaking of York West particularly, because that is my

Redistribution
5595'
own seat, but I should like to give the populations of the four Yorks according to the 1941 census. They are:
York North	 47,678
York South	 78.167
York East	 78,584
York West	 69,089
A very rapid change in population has taken place since 1941. I submit that it would have been in the interests of proper representation in this house if some consideration had been given by the committee to the shift in population which has occurred since the 1941 census. The year 1941 was a war year, and there had been great shifts of population due to war industry and other reasons. That census perhaps did not give a true picture of the population of Canada. Some areas had grown and were growing on a temporary basis because of special industries which it was obvious would be disbanded after the war. I am thinking of Nobel which has been almost completely abandoned since that war industry closed down.
In many suburban districts, such as the one which I have the honour to represent, the population shift has been of a permanent nature, and it is still going on. I should like to refer to what has happened in York West. May I say here that in many ways I would welcome the addition of the town of Weston to York West. I have many friends there and I think the war effort of Weston was equal to any town of its size in Canada. There is one other slight reason why it might be considered as part of the riding. Weston and Mimico are arch enemies in the ancient Canadian game of lacrosse and it will be nice to have them in a single constituency.
Be that as it may, this is the situation with regard to population. In 1941 York West had a population of 69,089, and by 1945 that had grown to 82,656, an increase of 13,567. I am taking these figures out of the Toronto municipal year book for 1946. I think the committee will be interested in these figures because they show what is happening in the area around Toronto. York township has a population of 82.753. We usually consider that there is a proportion of three to five as between York West and York South, which would give York West an addition of some 30,133. The other population figures are:
Etobicoke	 21,402
New Toronto	 10,173
Mimico	   8,785
Swansea	 7.217
Long Branch	 5.059
Weston	   6,377
When you add the population of Weston you reach a total population, during the election year 1945, of approximately 89.000 83166-357J
people. Let us assume that the growth is continuous, and I assure you, Mr. Chairman, that the growth is continuing and approximately at the same rate. Therefore we can expect to find an average annual increase of approximately 5,000 people for some years in that riding. This means that in this year the constituency of York West with the town of Weston will have a population approaching 100,000; and, with the growth continuing, by the time the next election comes round it will have the amazing population of approximately
110,000.	We in the large urban centres of population should be expected and be prepared to represent a greater number of people than the rural parts of the country. But here you have a population in 1949 of more than twice that of York North. I think that is extremely unfair. I think it is a maladjustment of representation in this house.
I want to go a little farther, and give the population of urban Toronto versus Toronto city itself, and I am giving the figures for 1945. I do not include in them those parts of the riding of York North which are purely rural, Vaughan, Whitchurch, King and Gwil-limburg townships, and the towns of Newmarket, Richmond Hill, Woodbridge, Aurora, which are all rural areas. The population of suburban municipalities adjoining Toronto for the year 1945-I am taking these figures from the 1946 Year Book, which is the most recent- was 260,689 versus a population in Toronto of 681,802. The suburban population reside mostly in York South, York East, York West. That is, three members of this house represent nearly 260,000 people. Actually York North has 26,000 of the 260,000, so that about 240,000 would be represented by three members of this house, which would mean that in the year 1945 the representation for the three Yorks which are nearest Toronto averaged 80,000 people per member. That, I think, should have been given more consideration by the committee. Here we have a permanently growing urban area of Ontario which, it is forecast, is going to grow at an even faster rate in the years to come, represented by only three members. Certainly some consideration should have been given to creating: another York.
It has been said that York North was kept as a rural seat. I cannot agree with this argument, because York North is very similar to the other Yorks. It has industries and, while it takes in a larger territory, there are large parts in both York East and York West which are entirely rural and where the people are engaged in farming and market gardening. So I say that, had this change been necessary, some consideration should
Redistribution

have been given to equalizing the four Yorks in population; that is, bringing the population of York North more into line with the population of the other three Yorks.
Let us see-and I think this is interesting- how this compares with some other ridings. I think the largest riding in Ontario will still be Welland, although I am not sure.
I am not complaining of representing a very large riding. I think it is a great honour to represent a very large riding, but the case of Welland is probably equal to the case I am putting up.
In 1945 the electors on the list in York West numbered 49,042. The electors on the list in Glengarry, which is the smallest riding -I do not say that York West is the biggest -numbered 10,649. In other words, York West has five times the number of electors in Glengarry. There is pretty nearly a five-times differential between the smallest riding of Glengarry and York West, which is a large riding, and now to that five-times differential we are adding the town of Weston, which in 1945 had 4,767 electors on the list, or nearly fifty per cent of the number of electors on the list in Glengarry. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that is not a true and proper representation of population in this House of Commons. I say that more consideration should have been given by the committee to a just equilibrium in the representation.
I have given the population of the town of Mimico as 8,785. Today, so I was informed recently by the mayor of the town, Mimico has a population of over 10,000. New Toronto has a population of over 10,000 and Etobicoke township, I am informed, has a population of 27,000 at the present time. I have not official figures, but these are figures given me by word of mouth by responsible officials in the various municipalities.
I consider that there is shocking discrepancy in the representation as brought down by this committee. I feel that the member for York West, in the twenty-first parliament, will be representing, at the beginning, 110,000 people, and if the growth goes on, at the end he will be representing probably 120,000 or 125,000 people. Compare that with Glengarry of
18,000,	a static population, and we get a discrepancy of over six to one. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that is out of line with a proper differential between an urban and a rural seat. I believe that the committee have failed, for reasons best known to themselves, to take proper consideration of the population discrepancy which many of the large industrial ridings of Ontario will be forced to face.

I have listened with keen interest to the debate which has taken place this afternoon. While, from the point of view of Alberta, there is little that I can add by way of protest, yet there is something I should like to say that has arisen from the speeches of some of the hon. members, and from the details and facts in the bill.
The Alberta subcommittee, under the able chairmanship of the hon. member for Atha-baska, did a very fine job. Their relations from the beginning were harmonious. They worked quickly and with predetermined intent and were able to get their work done to the satisfaction of all concerned. They gave what I think should have been a good lead and demonstration to the subcommittees of the other provinces on how to deal with this whole matter of redistribution at this time.
The Alberta subcommittee recommended no changes in this present bill for several good reasons. In the first place, the number of constituencies in the province was to remain exactly as before, seventeen. In the second place, there can be a matter of only three years until the next decennial census is taken, which will provide the basis for a new distribution of seats.

I had not intended saying very much about this; but as I sat and listened to the all too patent political moves being made I could not resist the opportunity to register my vehement protest over the thing that has been done.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I am not going to spend a great deal of time on this matter on this occasion for when the schedules come up I intend to have more to say than in these my opening remarks. I will direct my appeal today not to the house but to the Prime Minister of the country. As he said in 1932 my appeal goes to Caesar. I was very much surprised when he said this afternoon that he had no idea regarding what this committee had done or the recommendations that it had made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: My hon. friend is not quoting me correctly. I did not say I had not any knowledge of what the committee had done or of its recommendations. I said I had not interfered in any way with the committee while it was at its work or tried to influence its members.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I hasten to accept the correction. Then the Prime Minister does know what has been done.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Well, he reads the bills.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Yes; he knows what has been done. In view of that fact, many of the things I would have said, it becomes unnecessary for me to place before this committee and the country. My hon. friend the member for Peace River suggested that someone might endeavour to explain what was done as being a matter of coincidence. Mr. Chairman, coincidence becomes conspiracy -when it is repeated over and over again. I suggest at this time that if it is coincidence, then never before has coincidence in the matter of redistribution resulted in the position that those who are gerrymandered out of their constituencies are leaders in an opposition party. I would point out that the leader of the opposition, the president of the Progressive Conservative Association of Canada, and the president of the Young Progressive Conservative Association are of those whose constituencies are interfered with. I ask you, sir, how did it come about that these are the persons whose seats have been marked out for interference-interference, did I say? -annihilation in so far as the leader of the opposition is concerned.
I am going to speak now of my own constituency. The constituency of Lake Centre is surrounded by more constituencies than any other riding in the dominion-ten in number. Naturally it was felt that changes would be made in Saskatchewan. Naturally, when the reduction in the number of members by one took place, changes would have to be made. But, sir, how can the government explain the manner in which it went about the changes so far as Lake Centre is concerned? I make my appeal, not to the head of the committee, not to a committee for the province of Saskatchewan. I am making my appeal to Caesar himself.
This is what was done. It was necessary to increase the population of Lake Centre. It may be only a coincidence, but the first plan removed from the south end of the constituency of Lake Centre twenty-three townships. It may be only coincidence that these twenty-three townships returned a substantial Progressive Conservative majority in 1945. Then, in the northwest corner-I am speaking of the original plan-two townships were to be removed, one of which contained the largest town in the constituency, namely the town of Watrous. The makers of the plan removed a number of 'townships on the west side-seven townships on the west side of the constituency, in which there was a small majority for the C.C.F. candidate in the elec-

Redistribution
tion of 1945. It is said that they made these changes to increase the population of Lake Centre, and they commenced to increase the population by immediately removing twenty-three townships from the south side of the constituency, seven on the west side and two off the northwest corner.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Townships.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Townships, as my leader points out. Then, on the east side of the constituency sixteen townships were added out of the constituency represented by the Minister of Agriculture. It is again merely a coincidence that those sixteen townships returned a substantial majority for the C.C.F. candidate as against the Minister of Agriculture in the last federal election.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: That seems to be the hon. member's main trouble.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Then a portion was added from Yorkton constituency. I would not argue about those additions, and I would accept the plan as it is if there were missing from the plan an addition on the north side of the constituency. They removed from the bottom; they removed from the sides; they added on the east side and then finally added in the northeast corner of the constituency three townships out of the constituency of Humboldt. Never have those townships been in Lake Centre or in its predecessor, Last Mountain constituency. As a matter of fact, in winter time it will be impossible to get to the three unless one travels into Saskatoon, a distance of 140 miles. They have always been in Humboldt. They are connected directly through Humboldt, on a line of railway passing through the constituency; and yet they have been added to the constituency of Lake Centre. I am not here for the purpose of asking for consideration, but I am here to ask for justice. I am going to ask for justice from the Prime Minister, as he asked for justice in 1932.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: He did not get it.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I am not here to defend. The right hon. gentleman pointed out the situation in Prince Albert, namely, that
6.000	of his electors on the south side of that constituency had been removed and' were joined to the constituency of Rosthern. He pointed out to the then prime minister that what was planned was wrong and unfair. He said that it transformed a majority for him in Prince Albert constituency of some 1,100 into a minority of 600 odd. He said it was obvious that it had been done for a purpose; he appealed to the government of the day, in the interests of the preservation of the principle of fairness, a principle inherent in parliamentary government, to change the plan and it was changed. Sir, I point out what has been done in this constituency of Lake Centre in the area where a Progressive Conservative majority was given in the last election. It has been removed and to Lake Centre has been added a voting strength of 4,900, of whom only 286 were Progressive Conservatives in the last election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Did I understand my hon. friend to say that a change was made in Prince Albert?

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I should like to know the extent of it.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I have the Prime Minister's own admission before me, or rather his thanks to the government for having made the change. He points out on May 27, 1933, after having debated the matter in the house for a period of five dayis, that changes had been made, and he says, as reported at page 5559 of Hansard for that year:
I have made my appeal to Caesar, and I propose to abide by the decision Which has been given and not argue the matter further.
Then he went on to point out that a change was made in the southern portion of the constituency which altered the original plan, and he spoke his appreciation on behalf of the constituency of Prince Albert to the government for having made the change. The Prime Minister is now conversant with this matter. He can see the picture in the constituency of Kamloops. He can see the situation-and he knew of it before-in so far as the leader of this party is concerned, as a result of joining two Progressive Conservative seats in Manitoba. Is Portage la Prairie to be penalized because in a by-election it defeated the government candidate? Is that one of the reasons why Pontiac is being altered as well? Are they being penalized because in by-elections each defeated the government condidate?
There is nothing sacrosanct about the findings of a committee. In committee there was an agreement in so far as Nova Scotia was concerned. It was agreed that there should be two seats in Nova Scotia created for Halifax, one a city and one a rural seat. Was there anything sacrosanct about it? The day before yesterday we were advised in Halifax, that the government had decided not to follow the recommendations of the committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Advised by whom?
Redistribution

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: We were informed by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) on Saturday last, that the- government had decided not to follow the unanimous recommendation of the committee. I do not argue that question at all in so far as Halifax is concerned. I understand the situation there. But if there was nothing sacrosanct about an agreement on the part of the members of the committee in so far as Nova Scotia is concerned, why should others be about the findings of the committee where any other part of this country is concerned? I am asking the Prime Minister to reconsider the matter. In 1932 he pointed out that nothing was more dangerous to the public life of the country than to bring in what he called a gerrymandering measure in the last days of the session. It undermined democracy, it was a dangerous proceeding, and, regardless of whether parliament was to prorogue within the next day or so as planned, he and those associated with him intended to fight until they obtained justice.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: He did not get it.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I will deal with that question a little later on. I wish to adopt the definition of "gerrymander" as given by the right hon. gentleman at page 5276 of Hansard of 1932-33:
The word "gerrymander" in political parlance simply means that in redistributing a constituency the boundary lines are so altered as to do an obvious injury to one political party and give an obvious unfair political advantage to another party.
That defines what a gerrymander is. Tell me what justification there is to take away township after township from a constituency and then say that it is necessary in order to bring up the population and make it equal to that of constituencies adjoining it, to add on other parts of other constituencies?

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Why did the hon. member recommend it to the committee?

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: There is a fine question; I have heard that before. It was once raised as a defence by a highwayman who stuck a gun into the face of a victim and said, "Your money or your life"; and then afterwards said, when charged, "Why did he consent?"

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Did the hon. member not sign the recommendation?

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: That was exactly my position in so far as that committee report was concerned.

speechtext: Six o'clock.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Will some minister advise what, the government has for us this evening?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: At seven o'clock it is proposed to take up private bills. When they are disposed of we shall resume the debate on Bill No. 453, to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act. After that is disposed of we shall go into supply.

speechtext: What department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Fisheries.

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: We shall not go on with this tonight?

maintopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

No; tomorrow.
Progress reported.

Mr. RALPH MAYBANIi (Winnipeg South Centre):	Mr. Speaker, I wish at the outset
to advert to certain remarks made in the chamber this afternoon by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). The hon. member made reference to a certain brief. He said it had been stated in the committee that the individual in question had not filed a brief before the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation when, in fact, he had. I have no comment to make one way or another upon his estimate of the value of the evidence given in the committee in answer to his questions, any more than to say that it is very easy to wait until a witness who has given evidence, which you do not like, is gone, and then charge him in his absence, at a time when he cannot defend himself, with endeavouring to withhold information from the committee. There was plenty of opportunity in the committee for that to be done if such was the intention of the hon. member. My only reason for drawing the attention of the house to that matter is that I consider it very cheap business to attack people who cannot defend themselves. What is quite different is 'the attempted charge made by the hon. member for Kamloops against an individual who can defend himself, and I shall speak of that for just a few moments.
I speaking about this brief, ithe hon. member read a letter. He gave the date of the letter; he did not actually say that I had received that letter and that brief in time to present it to the committee. But, up to the moment that I rose to ask him a question, I think it was clear in the mind of every person in this house that what he was endeavouring to convey was, that I had received this document in time to have presented it to the committee, and, that I had not done so. Whether he intended that or whether he did not intend that, I am sure it was clear to every person in the house. The manner in which he described the incident was such as to imply that the chairman of the committee had deliberately refrained from allowing the committee to consider that particular brief. I do not wish to say any more about that except what I indicated this afternoon, that there is utterly no truth in that suggestion.

Thank you, Mr. Spe'aker. As you will readily understand, I was not arguing at all. I was just being interrupted frequently with meaningless expressions. I merely wish to make it clear that no document was placed in my hands at any time when it was possible for it to be brought before the committee, and then, not given to the committee.
Having disposed of that, I want to turn to something else which has come up in the course of this debate. A great many detail items have been dealt with, and perhaps it might be well to mention one or two of them iii passing, but I submit that the main idea in connection with the radio report and underlying this bill has not been touched on at all as yet, although from time to time members of the house on all sides profess to be agreed on this particular point.
Before dealing with that, I wish to refer to something that was said by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) in the course of his remarks. He made reference to the Cana-dan Broadcasting Corporation going "in the red", losing money, and11 think similar remarks were made by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). We ought to remember, Mr. Speaker, that the financial record of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not a bad one but rather that it is a very good one. It will be recalled that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation started out in the 1930's. It had no money to start with and borrowed money for capital improvements. The corporation paid1 all that money back with interest before payment was due. The record of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in. a financial way is a very good one. We should remember that during the war there was a period when licence fees fell off. We should remember that licences ddd not increase year by year but became fewer, owing to the fact that radios could not be bought. It was in these circumstances that the corporation came to the point where there was a deficit in income. To any person who wants to be fair about the record-and I am not suggesting that the hon. members for Eglinton or Lethbridge did not desire to be fair; I say that they did not present quite comprehensive enough a picture in just making a few remarks about the corporation being "in the red"- the main point to keep in mind with reference to the financial record o'f the corporation is that it is good, not bad.
Canadian Broadcasting Act

While I am on the subject, I wish to refer to what the hon. member for Lethbridge had to say.

I am sorry. I sometimes remember people coming from the places they mention and I keep on thinking of the hon. member for Macleod as coming from the fine city of Lethbridge, but I am sure he will not take offence. I shall try to be more accurate in the future. He made references to the financial record of the C.B.C. and at the same time spoke about the amount of money the private companies made. He spoke as if he thought what was in the report was a charge against the private companies for making so much money, and suggested, I think, that it was surely no crime to make money. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that to look at the report that way is to miss the whole point of that part of the report which deals with the financial records of the private companies. The report in that regard points out only that these companies would appear to be making a good deal of money and not paying a very large licence fee. After all, that is all it states. The report says there is a possibility the companies are making as many millions as are there disclosed, and making such profits by reason of the fact that they are granted a piece of a monopoly, and that it is quite possible private broadcasters are not paying as much as they ought to pay for the privilege of monopolistically giving out news and other forms of broadcasting over the air. I do not know what the position of the socialists may be, but I believe no person on this side objects to the private broadcasters making a good living, making a good return on their capital. As far as I am concerned, I am only too happy to see them doing well. However, if these companies are making a great deal of money by carrying on their particular type of radio broadcasting, and at the same time are getting certain benefits which come from the broadcast operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is paid for largely by public money, it is not unreasonable to suggest that they should pay a higher licence fee. That is all there is to that part of the report. Certainly, for any person to cavil about it, seems to me, with all respect, to be rather unreasonable. Indeed, if the report, on insufficient evidence, said these men are not paying enough for their privilege; if it said that on insufficient evidence, of course the right of criticism would be there-I think the duty of criticism would be there-and I should hope that I would never set my name to a report that said any 
such thing as that. But it is quite clear that what the report does in fact say. It says what I have already indicated, namely, that it is quite possible these people ought to be paying more money. That is as far as it goes.
