Many other statements have been made in the course of the debate. To mention many of them would take up too much time. I come to whait I consider to be the real point at issue in all 'these radio debates. But first, I should like to say that I consider this committee has been acting as a policy committee instead of as a budgeting committee in the last couple of years. I submit, sir, that the real purpose of this committee is to examine the financial affairs of the corporation in just 'the way another committee examines the affairs of 'the Canadian National Railways. In the Canadian National Railways committee we never undertake to declare policy. Last year and this year we have been going much farther afield than I submit the committee should, and for this reason, if no other, that we are not as well equipped as a cabinet to determine the policy, and we have not at our hands the great deal of technical information that we ought to have. I have no complaint about the work that has been put upon us, but I believe people are likely to get the wrong idea about the nature of this committee's work. It does seem to me that if the committee is to make policy we shall be changing the whole legislative structure of the parliament of Canada
and we shall have government by committee instead of by council. I submit that is not wise.
But whether we have the right to make policy or not, as members of parliament we certainly have the right to discuss it, and the question that has to be settled in all our minds here is this very simple one which came up in 1932 and earlier: "Is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to be the favoured instrument of broadcasting in this country? Is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to be the supreme chain broadcaster, or is it not? Are private stations to be allowed to exist and fulfil a community need, or are they to be allowed to expand into networks of national broadcasting?"
That is the thing that was basic when this institution was set up, and it still is. There is the consideration which has determined the committee, as to whether it would or would not recommend in favour of a regulatory body. Believing that for the reason that ithe Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is robust in the service of Canada, and that that is the main point at issue, 'the committee concluded that the easiest way of effecting that was to have the CB.C. continue to exercise the functions it is exercising today.
I personally would have no objection to a regulatory board. I am not so strongly for it, but I would have no objections to it. If, however, I were writing a law establishing a regulatory body I would write it in such a way that it would be entrammeled about so that it could not do anything to injure the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That is the crux. For example, I would entrammel it in the same way as the transport board is hindered from touching grain rates in western Canada. But of course what we had put before us was nothing of that sort. What we had put before us, and what the Tories promptly espoused, was the creation of a board which would be appointed by parliament and could be touched only by parliament, a board whose affairs could be reviewed only by parliament, subject to both houses of parliament, a body which should have all the powers possessed by the transport department and those possessed by the broadcasting corporation. In fact, they wanted to set up another body as strong as parliament, and when I learned that, I considered it would create a fascist organization.
Some persons, I believe the member for Macleod in particular, have made the statement that some members have their minds made up for them. The hon. member never spoke a truer word. Some people appeared
Canadian Broadcasting Act

to have their minds made up for them right from the beginning. In fact, from the very-second that the private broadcasters' brief was laid on the table, every Tory on the committee, and those associated with them, advocated that particular thing which was claimed in the brief. Their minds were made up for them all right. There is no question in the world about that. They came to the committee every day with prepared leading questions. If they were not briefed every evening they acted as if they were, and it shows how quick they were to pick up the point of view of those who desire to obtain private monopoly over radio. That is the position they took, and we might as well have this issue between the Tories and us cleared up now. The case is not one of socialism; it is not a case of government ownership of some industry which is usually run by private persons. This is a question as to whether or not we should control a monopoly, and on that I feel there should not be any doubt, any more than Mr. Bennett had doubt at the time he originally proposed the national set-up.
We have kept a monopoly over broadcasting, what I call country-wide broadcasting
that is, the network-and if the Tories now want to turn back and eat their own child, as some animals do, all right. Let us have the proposition clear, that the real issue in this matter is whether we shall have a private monopolistic network broadcasting or whether we shall not. All other matters fall into pale insignificance compared with that.
We can have a regulatory body as long as it is understood that the robustness of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation continues. We can have anything as long as we are first of all agreed upon something upon which we were at one time all agreed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, while there are numerous subjects which are germane to the motion before us and which might be discussed, I know it is the desire to get on with other legislation. I am probably like the fellow who proposed to his girl and when she asked him why he did not say something more he replied that he had probably said too darned much already.

The question which I propose to discuss for a few minutes was raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank): Is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to be the supreme broadcasting authority?

The radio fee was to enable this national instrument to provide better radio service. Now what is better radio service? I think Mr. Speaker, that better radio service must, in the final analysis, boil d'owm, to this-the service that is most acceptable to the Canadian radio listener.
I do not think we can say what is better theatre, what is better opera, what is better painting. The public must be the judge of what is better theatre, what are better methods, what is better public entertainment.

Here we have two privately owned stations, according to an independent survey, out-listening and out-selling the C.B.C. stations; here we have them providing, on the basis of an independent survey, better service, and service of interest to the listening public, than the C.B.C. stations in the Toronto area, both of which are key stations for networks.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, who is providing the service? Are the private stations providing the service, or are the C.B.C. stations providing the service? Those who want to listen to CBL in the evening were 13-9 per cent; to CJBC, 4-6 per cent; to CFRB, 35 per cent; and to CKEY, 23 per cent. Those are the figures for the independent stations. But we come to another factor which is significant. We come to the fact that in Toronto, as in many other places, there is competition from the United States stations. I would just mention one, WBEN in Buffalo: in the morning, 5-5 per cent; in the afternoon, 8-6 per cent, and in the evening, 11-3 per cent. Here is a situation which surely shows that something
is wrong with the C.B.C. This air is free. There is a preference of the people who are listening to the United States station, three to one, over the key stations of the dominion network. I have not said what is good and what is bad. Surely what is good must be based on what people want to listen to. It may be that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation programmes are more intellectual, with higher quality music; but the question is, do they draw the listeners? I do not think there can be any other yardstick. From people who listen to the radio I understand that there are just as many soap operas and just as much, to use a better word, ballyhoo, on the C.B.C. emanation as there is on the private stations, particularly the United States private stations. I suggest that, before these powers are given to the C.B.C., considerable searching should be done.

Mr. Speaker, in closing the debate I should like to make a few brief remarks about some of the things which have already been said in this discussion. It is generally known and understood that radio in this country and elsewhere is one of the big prizes in the current struggle for power by reactionary private enterprise. An agitation has been carried on in Canada as it has been carried on in the United States. Here an unscrupulous campaign has been carried on in an attempt to discredit the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and at the same time to expand commercialism.
During the debate I have been struck by the short memories of some hon. members opposite. For instance, several members of the Progressive Conservative party have said that they thought some new and separate board should be set up to regulate and license broadcasting. They are forgetting a basic principle to which their party long held, and which is that all broadcasting should be coordinated under a national system, for which purpose we must have some regulating power.
Let me say that there is nothing new about that principle. It was first established by par-

liament when the last Conservative government was in power. It was embodied in the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act of 1932. A commission was set up under that act, a commission which had even broader powers than the present corporation.
The main change in the act of 1936 was to set up a corporation to be independent of the government in carrying out the functions laid down, instead of the old commission set up by the Conservative government under the act of 1932, which had been right under the thumb of the government of that day.
In the following years, successive parliamentary committees reaffirmed the principle, and with the concurrence of Conservative members who were on the committees. I well remember that, because I had the honour of being chairman for several years of the committee investigating radio broadcasting.
In the last two years, certain private radio interests have been campaigning for a change in radio laws which they think would give them more freedom to make profit and to exploit the public through channels which they have been allowed to use. Some of my hon. friends seem to have decided to forget the principles of their party, have repudiated them, and have allowed themselves to become the champions of private interests. I presume that members of the Progressive Conservative party have been speaking for themselves, because neither this year nor last year, when a similar debate took place, have I heard the leader of that party declare as to what was the policy of the Progressive Conservative party.
Tonight when he spoke he referred to the fee. I believe that his criticism was entirely unfounded and that he has not the right idea with reference to how the matter will be handled. He said, as is correct, that there should be an appropriation bill for this amount of money. There will be. Each year there will be; and it will be in the estimates in order to cover the costs of administration. Probably this year, since it is too late for that estimate to come in the supplementary estimates it will appear in the further supplementary estimates which will be brought down at the end of the fiscal year. Each year there will have to be voted by parliament, and it will go into the appropriation bill, an amount of money to cover the costs of administration and of collection. So that I submit there will be an opportunity for discussion in parliament yearly with respect to matters pertaining to costs of collection and administration.
I want to reassert that the Liberal party has a distinct and clear policy with respect to

Canadian Broadcasting Act
radio in Canada. We believe in a nationally owned, nationally controlled and nationally operated system of radio for all the people of this country. It will be nationally operated by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and nationally controlled by them, a corporation responsible not to the government but to parliament. That is a clear-cut definition of the policy of the Liberal party with respect to national radio; and I have yet to hear from the leader of the Progressive Conservative party what the policy of his party is on 'this matter. Every man in the party has a policy of his own as it suits his own interests or the interests of those for whom he is speaking.

On the development of C.B.C. facilities, members of the Progressive Conservative party also seem to have very short memories. Plans for further high-powered stations to use these channels were stated publicly and were approved by parliamentary committees in the reports of which Progressive Conservative members have concurred.
During the war, naturally the corporation was unable to continue development of its technical facilities. It was absolutely impossible to get the transmitters and other technical equipment which would have been necessary in those years to carry on the expansion we had in view. Certain private stations, under the circumstances, were allowed to use these wave lengths provisionally at low power. Now some members of the opposition call it legalized robbery when the C.B.C. goes ahead with the original plans to make use of these wave lengths at high power.
I submit that it would be legalized betrayal of the Canadian people who own the national radio system if we did not proceed with the programme which we had in view prior to the war, and which was interrupted because of the war. It would be a legalized selling out of the public interest to certain private organizations if they were allowed to develop these clear channels at high power, instead of the national system, as ivas originally intended.

During the war, when the demand for canned fish and other foods was great, it was noticeable on the Atlantic coast that, to a certain extent, quality was neglected for the sake of quantity. speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister whether he has given any further consideration to implementing the recommendation made to him by Mr. Harris Johnstone on December 7, 1945, with respect to the dispute over certain Canadian Pacific railway pension rates. It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to speak at length on this matter as I have done on previous occasions, because the house and the government are fully aware of the situation. I notice there was a little bit of applause-but very little- when I said I was not going to speak at length, but actually, Mr. Chairman, I regard this matter as a great deal more important than some of the matters this house has found time to devote -its attention to in the dying days of this session.
The minister knows that, following representations to the government on this matter from the trade unions affected and representations made on the floor of this house, he appointed one of his officials to make a *thorough investigation of the whole question. That official Mr. H. S. Johnstone, made a report to the minister in December, 1945. That report, including its appendices, runs to some sixty-six pages and the concluding paragraph of the report is a definite and specific recommendation to the minister 'that a royal commission be appointed.
I may point out to the minister and to the members who are following me that this question differs from the subject matter of Bill No. 24, which has been before the house on another occasion; that bill has to do with an attempt to prevent this kind of thing from happening in the future. The royal commission asked for in Mr. Johnstone's report has to do with the actual dispute that still obtains 
over the pension rights lost by Canadian Pacific railway employees in 1918 and 1919. For these men there has 'been expressed on the floor of this house time and again a great deal of sympathy. The minister expresses his sympathy, the Prime Minister expresses his sympathy for these men, and it is a sympathy borne out of an experience he had with a similar situation some years ago. But the fact of the matter is that that sympathy has not proven of a great deal of assistance to these men. Their case, to my way of thinking, is air-tight. They were able to convince Mr. Johnstone thait they had a case and I do feel that the government should proceed to implement the recommendation made to them by Mr. Johnstone.
On previous occasions the minister, as well as indicating his sympathy, has made various comments. For one thing he said that the money in question was that of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and in reply to that I have called his attention to one paragraph in Mr. Johnstone's report which deals with that very point and suggests that the men had an equity and that their contention on that score was .well founded.
The minister has also said that on previous occasions he has consulted the Department of Justice to determine whether or not there would be any advantage in appointing a royal commission; he has given us the opinion of the Department of Justice that there would not be any advantage, and on the basis of that opinion he has declined thus far to appoint the royal commission. I submit that the responsibility in this matter rests with the minister himself and that he should not crawl out from under that responsibility by quoting the Department of Justice. The fact of the matter is that it might help to solve the problem if a royal commission were to go into this matter and to make a specific recommendation, even though that royal commission had not the authority to compel the implementing of that recommendation. But if a royal commission were appointed and went into this matter, I am satisfied that its finding would be on the side of the men and that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company would find that public support would be such as to compel them to pay some attention to the report of the royal commission. I know that the Minister of Labour has had to think of this matter a good many times, because I have drawn it to his attention repeatedly and he has had a great deal of correspondence about it from men representing the unions concerned.
When the Prime Minister made the promise back in 1945 to have the question investi-

Supply-Labour
gated so as to determine whether or not a royal commission should be appointed, an obligation was thereby incurred to carry out the result of the preliminary investigation. I point out again that that preliminary investigation was made, not by a person prejudiced in favour of the men or prejudiced in favour of the company; it was carried out by an appointee of the Department of Labour. That appointee interviewed the employees' organizations. He interviewed all the companies concerned, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Canadian Pacific Express Company, the Canadian Pacific Steamships. He also interviewed other employers who had been involved in the 1919 strike and had subsequently reinstated the pension rights of their employees, such as the Canadian National Railways, the police department of the city of Winnipeg, the Manitoba telephone system, the post office and other similar large employers. Thus his finding was in the nature of an objective finding about the situation. As I say, he not only answers the usual arguments put up against the case of the men, but concludes with a specific recommendation to the minister that a royal commission be appointed.
That specific recommendation which is contained in the concluding paragraph should be read, of course, in conjunction with the opening paragraph in which Mr. Johnstone says to the minister, "You appointed me to do this task for the specific purpose of concluding with a recommendation one way or the other as to whether or not there should be this royal commission; my recommendation is in the affirmative." I make my appeal once more to the Minister of Labour on behalf of these men to take this step and have this royal commission established.
The only opportunity there has been in this house for a debate coming close to this question was on the bill to which I referred previously when there was wide support for the purpose and the intent of that bill. That bill went to the standing committee on industrial relations. That committee studied it with representations from both sides, and made a report back to this house which was concurred in a few days ago. I admit it was a rather pious statement, but * at least it was pious on the right side. It said that the purpose of the bill commended itself to the committee but that further study should be gone into. To my way of thinking, it is clear that people who have any humanitarian interest at all, any interest in justice, feel that these men have a case. We are not asking the government to pour out money; we are not asking the government to do any-83166-3594
thing out of the way. We are simply asking that they carry out the recommendation of one of their own officials and appoint a royal commission to look into this whole matter.

By the very nature of things I take the advice of the legal officers of the crown. 1 am not going to speak at length on the subject; I did so last year. My hon. friend knows the background, and he knows I do not think there is any hon. member in the house who would not be fair to anybody, irrespective of whether they were employees or employers, in a matter similar to this. As I say, the law officers of the crown have advised against it. We have accepted their advice and that is how the matter stands.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I should like to know what the minister means by his sympathy for these men if he is prepared to do nothing for them.

I do not know whether I should say what I was going to say. I was fighting for the working class before you ever knew there was a working class in this country. I do not think it is necessary to say these things to an individual like myself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It seems to be.

I was in the labour movement before you knew anybody interested in them. I am talking about trade unions. I do not think it is fair for my hon. friend to say things like that. When he searches his conscience he will know it is not fair himself, at least if he has any conscience.

I should like to say one word on this point. Perhaps what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said did not seem fair to the minister, but certainly it has not been improved by what the minister has said. To refer to the fact that you were
Supply-Labour

in the labour movement before the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was born does not mean anything except that you were born before he was.
I did not say that.
That is something neither one of you had anything to do with.
Thank goodness.

You just arrived when you arrived. What I wish to point out to the minister is this. I do not know exactly what recommendation the Department of Justice made with respect to the appointment of a royal commission; but the appointment of a royal commission is not a matter that has legal implications any more than the appointment of a commissioner by the Minister of Labour. Therefore it seems to me that the minister is falling back on the fact that the Department of Justice said that perhaps something could not be done even if a royal commission was appointed. But here is a case where the minister can take the responsibility of appointing a royal commission. If the royal commission made a decision in one way, then the employees concerned would have their case strengthened. If it made it the other way, I suppose the employees concerned will have no further basis to carry on their agitation to have their grievance rectified. In my opinion it is really too bad that the Minister of Labour did not exercise his rights and ask that a royal commission be appointed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Has the minister either before him or in his mind the exact details of the opinion that he got from the Department of Justice?
The answer is no.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I remember very well what the minister told me last year when he had just got the ruling from the Department of Justice. It was to the effect that in the opinion of the department it would not serve any useful purpose. That is quite a different thing from the Department of Justice saying that there is no legal basis for establishing the royal commission. Bearing in mind his responsibility to these men, I contend that the minister has no right to fall back on an opinion of that kind of the Department of Justice. I contend that it is his responsibility to face up to the question as to whether or not a royal commission would do some good. I submit that my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, has put the case pointedly. The royal commission would do one or the other of two things. It would either take the negative side of it and sav that, these 
men have no case, and that would be the end of it, or it would say that these men have a case and then it would be up to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to consider the effect of public opinion on their failure to carry out the recommendation of the royal commission.
The minister gets a little bit worried about the statements which he thinks are a bit unfair to him, which are made on the floor of this house. I wonder what he would think about the statements that some of the men affected make outside this house about his attitude. They feel that he is completely unfair to them; that he is taking the side of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, talking sympathy but failing to express it at all so far as the rights of these men are concerned. It has been a long long battle, but these men who are still living do not feel like giving up yet; they will continue their strugggle for their rights until they win.
I have referred before, but I refer again, to a similar battle that was carried on in this country years ago when the present Prime Minister took up the cudgels on behalf of men who were similarly deprived of their pension rights in 1910. I submit that this is on all fours with that and that the government of the day, being still under the same Prime Minister, should be consistent wdth the stand it took before and take up the cudgels on behalf of these men by at least appointing this royal commission.
My hon. friend talks about experts, and he and his associates lean on experts. Whatever an expert is I do not know, but I will say, on a question of law, every man to his own last.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But this is not a question of law. This is a question of opinion on a labour matter, and I submit that even you are more of an expert than the Department of Justice on that.
If my hon. friend wants my frank opinion, he is leading these men up a blind alley and sand-bagging them for political reasons.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I will answer that.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And we will answer you back too.

The hon. member knows as well as I do that you cannot pass a law to spend other people's money-and that is what it amounts to-and I do not think it is fair to these men to try to fool them along and to say that by the appointment of some commission you can make this organization do that which they are not legally bound to do.

Sup-ply-Labour
I think it is unfair. I know the old story of accusing everybody who stands up in this house and tries to take an impartial view of things and to be fair, and to say that such people are fighting on the side of big interests. That is not the correct approach, and I say to my hon. friend, the member for Winnipeg North Centre, that if I want advice I shall take it from those who know what they are talking about.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am afraid the minister let the cat out of the bag. He made the statement a moment ago that I was leading these people up a blind alley and that I was doing it for political purposes. May I point out that it was on April 24, 1945, that Mr. M. M. MacLean, director of industrial relations, on behalf of the Minister of Labour, appointed Mr. Johnstone to make this investigation to determine whether or not a royal commission should be established.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There was an election on June 11, 1945. These men are getting the impression now that the appointment of Mr. Johnstone was just leading them up a blind alley in the period of the two months before the election of that year; and they are asking me, time and time again, if that is why this report, so favourable to them, is being shelved. There is a strange coincidence in that the appointment of the commissioner was made just before the election, but when the report comes down a few months after the election we find it difficult to get any action. Does that mean that when the next election comes along maybe we shall get some other device like this, leading these men up another blind1 alley?

In the event of unemployment increasing to any extent, will the labour department itself have any programme, or would it be allowed to have one, having regard to the functioning of the Department of Reconstruction, and1 Supply? The workers generally would look to the labour department, and the minister remembers very well that, in the days of the late Hon. Norman Rogers, that gentleman did' have a very good programme. Will the present labour department have any authority to initiate any programme to take care of unemployment?

That comes under reconstruction and supply. I am one of those optimistic individuals who do not look for serious unemployment in the near future. At the moment we have the highest peacetime employment in our history, and with good sense and good management it should continue. I know that some people are predicting hundreds of thousands out of work-
Wait a year and see.
and they take a Satanic delight in it.
No satanic delight at all. You have no policy and are making no preparations.
You don't know the half of it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is right.
Let the minister answer my question.
That comes under reconstruction and supply. The labour department is merely a placement organization.
It has nothing to do with initiating? That will be left with reconstruction?
Yes.

Human rights and
fundamental freedoms.

That is more than the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has done during the past few weeks. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I did not say that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

109.	Annuities Act, $568,195.

Do the people of Canada pay for the administration of the Annuities Act? If this is a service given to those who take out and pay for annuities, why should the people *of Canada have to pay commission to agents of $313,000 as shown on page 130 of the estimates? service, and pay in order to expand it? Is it not up to the people themselves to take out annuities, if they wish to, instead of, in a sense, our advertising this service and soliciting

As I said before, the back-bone of the nation are the thrifty people. I think the same will be true when most of the people who are advocating certain reforms have gone. I do not think it will change a great deal. The whole basis of the annuities plan was to have people prepare for old age at their own expense and by their own labour. It is not on a scale followed by the straight line insurance companies. I believe the maximum is $1,200 a year. However I think it is all to the good, and is a sound policy.

In days gone by, the government has seen fit to set the maximum at $1,200. The cost of living has increased so much that $1,200 no longer does anything like what it did in 1939. In comparison today we would find that it probably takes $2,000 or $2,400 for the same purposes.
I am a great believer in annuities, and I should like the minister to see whether or not his department would give consideration to raising the maximum to * at least $2,000 instead of $1,200.
While there is a certain expense involved in the administration of these annuities, nevertheless they do keep people off the old age pensions, and the amount which otherwise would have to be paid for that purpose is lowered. Although I do not expect the minister would have the information at hand, it would be interesting if he could tell the committee the amount saved yearly by reason of the fact that some old people have an income of $1,200, because of go\*ernment annuities, and therefore do not have to take the old age pensions.

was spent.

That is easily understandable when you have a high level of employment. It has been our experience, particularly with the returned men that they want to go straight into industry. There is not the urge to learn a trade, I am sorry to say, under conditions existing at the moment when we have an expanding economy. I do not know that you can do much about the

Supply-Labour
matter. Every province, without exception, has cooperated magnificently with the dominion in all these training plans.
None was refused a grant?
The relationship between my department and the different provinces is 100 per cent cooperation.
With regard to these payments to the provinces, I believe there is a grant for building purposes as well. Is that only for technical education as well?
That is another appropriation.
That has nothing to do with this?
No. I know what my hon. friend has in mind. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was speaking of the same thing.
The grant for building purposes applies to technical education?
Yes.

The minister has mentioned that there is relatively full employment at the present time and that young men do not want to serve apprenticeships. I would ask whether during the operation of this provision there had been any reluctance on the part of labour unions to allow apprentices to be trained in the various fields. I could not help but feel in the bad days of depression that vocational training of this kind would be a most wonderful thing, because many young lads could not find work and were simply idling away their time. I hope the department is in a position to extend this vocational training should a time come upon us again when there is not full employment.
The trade unions have cooperated to the fullest extent.
As much as you could wish?

I would say they have gone all out. I know Ontario because I live here, and I know the people who were associated with the establishment of the apprenticeship plan. I mention Mr. Joseph Pigott of Hamilton and Ernest Ingles of London and the late James Marsh, former deputy minister of labour of Ontario. They all cooperated with the government in the establishment of these plans in Ontario.

Item agreed to.
Vocational Training Coordination Act, 1942-
11.',. Expenses of vocational training advisory council, $4,000.

This is just for
travelling expenses?
Yes.
Where did the council meet last year?
It met in Ottawa about six weeks ago. I cannot say just when they met last year. I have a reputation for having a good memory, but I do not remember everything.

Am I right in understanding that the total appropriation under the previous item last year was not used? Would the minister also answer my question, if we run into a time when employment is not as high as it is today, is adequate provision being made for the training of young men who may not find jobs available?

That is a pretty difficult question to answer. I have my own personal views about expenditures by governments. I could not tell you what is going to happen this time next year. My own guess would be that we shall still have a high level of employment, but in these days, with international conditions as they are, he is a pretty wise man who would predict too far ahead.
You did not use the whole appropriation last year, only $264,000 out of $1,000,000?
That is right.

Item agreed to.
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940-
115. Administration, including expenditures incurred in connection with the activities of the national employment service as delegated by the Minister of Labour in accordance with section 88 of the act, $19,160,280.

There has been an increase of 521 employees on the staff of this branch and the salaries have gone up proportionately, by about $600,000. I should like to ascertain why such a large amount is required for temporary assistance; $13,517,930 is a lot of money for temporary assistance.

This scheme was established in 1941 during the war when, as my hon. friend knows, the percentage of permanent employees being taken on was low for obvious reasons. It was to give the men returning from overseas priority in civil service positions. The whole question of temporary employees is under study at the moment by the civil service commission.
Supply-Labour
The returned soldiers should certainly have priority in employment in the civil service, but $13,000,000 must cover a lot of employees and what is to become of the displacees?
Out of 7,985 employees, 6,889 were temporary.
And they are being released?
Not necessarily. There has not been the drive by the returned men to get into the civil service such as there was after the last war.
It is the right place to be. It is the softest place I know.
I never take a negative position on anything.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You must be on safe ground now, you are smiling.
I have been on safe ground all my life, particularly during the war years.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Not when you lose your temper.

I was not like some people who predicted for their own reasons that there would be half a million people out of employment six months after the war was over. I am not suggesting who they might have been, but I was convinced in my own judgment, and that judgment was vindicated, that we would have full employment after the war was over and for a long time to come if the world kept its feet on the ground and had the good sense to manage its affairs.
Can the minister tell the committee the number of persons covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act in 1946 and the number of persons covered now?
Say in June, 1946, and June, 1947, or the nearest months.
There are, in round figures, 2,600,000 now covered. We have not the 1946 figures, but I shall get them for my hon. friend.

This item would appear to indicate an increase of $11,278,000 for the year 1947-48; yet at the end of the estimates on page 133 in respect of demobilization and reconversion for the year 1946-47 there is an item for national unemployment service. Will the minister straighten me out with respect to this? What is the difference here?

The answer is this. Last year there were two votes, one in the demobilization vote and the other in the general administration vote for the unemployment insurance commission. This year both votes have been added together. That is the reason for the apparent increase. Actually there was a reduction of $259,720 in the expenditure for this year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister a question or two with respect to the position of married women, particularly here in Ottawa, and their relationship to unemployment insurance. I think I know something about the basis of unemployment insurance and appreciate the difficulty relating to their question; nevertheless I feel that they have a just complaint. As I say, I have in mind married women in Ottawa who were asked to take on temporary jobs during the war. Very soon after they found themselves in these jobs, they7 were asked to pay unemployment insurance. They asked to be exempted on the ground that their jobs were only temporary and that, when the war ended, they would be unemployed, even though, in part, by choice. They7 were told by7 the authorities that it would be necessary for them to pay unemployment insurance and that it would be to their advantage to do so. I am told that during 1945 and part of 1946 some of these women whose jobs came to an end were granted unemployment insurance when they met the usual conditions; that is, they had to be available for other work similar in character, and that work had to be unavailable for them. But I am told that this year, 1947, women who are being let out, when they apply for their unemployment insurance, are not treated in the same way that similar women were in the last two years. I am told that they are offered jobs not at all similar in character to the ones they7 had been in, and that when they are unwilling to take these dissimilar jobs at much low7er rates of pay they are told that they are thereby7 disqualified from receiving unemployment insurance.
I know that there is an actuarial basis to unemployment insurance, and that it is similar to fire insurance. You pay in, and if you are not so unfortunate as to have to collect, well, you really are fortunate. But these women feel that there is discrimination against them on two counts. On the one hand, because of what they were told when they were compelled to pay insurance, and, on the other, because of the more favourable treatment accorded women in similar circumstances who were let out of their jobs in 1945 and 1946.
I should like the minister to make some comment on that. I have no doubt that this

Supply-Labour
matter has been brought to the attention of his officials, and they know the answers that have been given and the dissatisfaction that these women have felt with the answers. I shall be glad if he will also say something about the situation in general at the present time.

May I answer the first question first? In the first place, of course the insurance is administered by the unemployment insurance commission with an impartial chairman and representatives of labour and of the employer. That is the insurance end of it. Then the act definitely stipulates that before you can draw insurance you must be available for employment. This is elementary in an insurance scheme of this description. With respect to the control that we have, there have been set up across the dominion courts of referees, composed of a chairman, a representative of labour and a representative of the employer. If any person considers that he has been unsatisfactorily dealt with or that the officials have not complied with the legislation he has the right to appeal to the court of referees in his locality; and, if he is not satisfied with that, the appeal can go to the umpire. As I said previously, it is generally known that both labour and the employers are represented on these courts of referees.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The difficulty seems to revolve around those words we discussed a year or two ago, "suitable employment", and also the way in which the matter is handled in the offices, in the replies that are madie by the people in these offices to the women themselves. For example, I have before me a number of cases about which information has been given to me. In the main they are the stories of married women who had become grade 2 or grade 3 stenographers and who were offered such positions as charwomen, assistants in laundries, ironers. work at slicing bread, icing cakes, baby sitting, housekeeping and so on. When they report that they are unwilling to take positions of this kind and feel that they should not be asked to take them within the meaning of the words "suitable employment", they are simply told by the people in the offices to whom they appeal that nothing can be done about the matter. They have also been told at times that the staff is inadequate to cope with the situation; that they are just now catching up with the married women. I pointed out to the minister previously that part of this problem is created by the more favourable treatment which some of the women got in 1945 and 1946. It is on that basis that the women being let out now consider they are suffering discrimination.
There is another point in connection with that. Can the minister table for the information of the committee the last directives to unemployment insurance offices with respect to the phrase "suitable employment"? We had a considerable discussion over this matter the session before last and, I believe, last session too. I am still receiving complaints, particularly from Winnipeg, to the effect that, on the basis of directives sent out to the unemployment offices, men who apply for unemployment insurance are being told that, after a short period, they must be prepared to accept employment at a five cent cut in salary and, after a further three weeks, they must be willing to accept a ten cent cut, and; so on. Back in the fall of 1945 when we first had a discussion about this matter the minister's argument was that you had to realize that peacetime rates of pay would be different from wartime rates. We are in a peacetime situation now; this practice seems to be going on, and it gives to many labour men the feeling that it is being used to depress wages. I should like to hear the minister's comments and I would also appreciate it if he would table the latest directives regarding terms of suitable employment.

I do not think any
member of a board of referees, or any man in his senses in an administrative position would deliberately lay himself open to the charge of depressing wages. I know many of these men who are on boards of referees. They were appointed under my jurisdiction and are well known from one end of Canada to the other. There is absolutely no intention, to my knowledge, of seeking to put such a policy into effect. This is an unemployment scheme and, while there is nearly $400 million in the fund, unless there is a proper administration you can soon wreck the fund.

It did not take long to
do it in England after the last war.

Of course it did not;
it went bankrupt. I would imagine there has been some difficulty in the demobilization of married women who entered commerce, agriculture and industry during the war. Many such women wish to go back home. In the great majority of cases they have found that home is better than industry. There has to be some regard to a condition of that kind in administering a policy such as this. My hon. friend referred to a directive. As a matter of fact, it is in the mail now on the way to his office. If he wants it put on the record I could put it on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am glad to know that it is on the way. I wrote and asked the
Su pply-Labo ur

deputy for it. Seeing that it has been laid on the table in previous sessions, I think it should be made a matter of public record.

The minister refers to
married women employed in industry who never hoped to collect unemployment insurance. Why should they be charged the same as those who remain in industry?
It is a simple principle. In life insurance you do not want to die in order to win. In fire insurance you do nett want your house to burn down in order to win; at least honest people do not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: With government annuities you live to win.

Yes. There must be
tens of thousands of people who will never draw a cent of unemployment insurance in their lifetime.
They know it now.

Yes. If I had my way I would provide that everyone should carry unemployment insurance, particularly members of parliament. The life expectancy of this job is rather short. Many people think that members are men of destiny, instead of ships that pass in the night. I have met ex-members of this house who have rendered yeoman service to the country and have gone the way of all members of parliament, often in destitute circumstances. You hear a great deal of talk about politicians, but I have never met a so-called politician who was not poorer at the end of the road for having been in the House of Commons.

This is a question that has given a good deal of trouble and I imagine it is a difficult one. Perhaps when the unemployment insurance scheme has been longer in operation we shall not have so many complaints. In a directive sent to me last year it is stated that in an occupation an offer at a wage rate of five cents an hour lower than the former rate might be considered suitable after three weeks of unemployment, and an offer at a wage rate of ten cents lower might (be considered suitable after four weeks of unemployment. Much would depend on the employment as well as on the rate of wages, but I have a case that was brought to my attention where a woman who had been earning $160 a month was disqualified because she refused to accept a job at $100. She appealed to the board of referees and they sustained the disqualification, not because she refused the position, but because she had placed a restriction of $125 a month on her services. The employment officer who gave evidence swore that no

positions for girls had boon listed at the office carrying a salary of $125 a month. I do not know what can be done. Here again it is a question of the kind of employment and whether a person should be kept indefinitely on unemployment insurance, or until the insurance is exhausted, before being disqualified for not taking employment at a lower rate of pay. Here is a large discrepancy of $60 a month. If it is the same kind of employment, it seems to me that, there is too much of a difference to justify the disqualification.

There are some rural postmasters who are not civil servants. They run post offices in small communities, and I know some who get a total income of $3,000 or possibly slightly more a year. In some cases, after appointment these postmasters get a girl to do the work while they carry on some other substantial business running into thousands of dollars of income a year. That is all wrong. It should not occur, but it does happen. My first question is this. Do the employees of rural postmasters who are actually in contract with the government come under the Unemployment Insurance Act? Second, will these same employees, who are employees of federal contractors, one might say, come under the terms of the present labour bill now being studied by a committee of the house?

I do not think the hon. member's second question comes under this vote. He is talking now about labour legislation. I do not know what this committee will do next year. You put a nickel in the slot and you do not know what is coming out. I could not answer that question. The hon. member would have to get some expert or some prognosticator to do that for him.
The minister said he was a pretty good prophet.
I imagine these other people would come under the act; that is, rural postal contractors. I could not say for certain, but I would imagine they came under the act.
How many are now drawing benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act?
I will get that.

Second, how many unfilled jobs are listed with the unemployment insurance commission? Third, how many unfilled applications are there for workers on farms? Will it be the policy of the unemployment insurance commission to require able-bodied

Privilege-Mr. Lacombe
single men who cannot find work elsewhere to take farm employment this year, as was done in the previous year?
There are a good number of questions there.
How many are drawing benefits, as of a recent date?
There are 39,966.
As of what date?
That is the last week of June. The other question was as to how many are registered.
How many unfilled jobs are listed with the commission? How many employers have sent in applications for employees?
I have that figure: 67,000 males; 40,000 females.

The other question was, how many unfilled jobs have been listed for farm work, and will the commission require able-bodied single men who cannot find work elsewhere to take work on farms during the harvest season?

I will make a note of that question, and if I can answer it, I will do so tomorrow. It looks as though I shall not get through these estimates tonight. Since a message has come from the senate, I move that the committee now rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

If it would not be too much trouble for the minister, I would ask him to put on Hansard a list of the provinces where the unfilled jobs are and where those receiving unemployment insurance benefits are. I would ask him to give a break-down and put it on Hansard.
I will do that tomorrow.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

subtopic: FREE CONFERENCE WITH THE SENATE IN VIEW OF AMENDMENTS TO BILL NO. 364

I have the honour to inform the house that a message has been received from the Senate agreeing to the free conference desired with the Senate for the purpose of communicating the reasons which induced the Commons not to concur in the amendments made by the Senate to Bill 3fi4. intituled ''An Act to amend the criminal code", and has appointed the bon.
Senators Robertson, Haig and Beauregard, as managers on their part at the said free conference.
